At the Campbeltown distillery, at 3:17 PM he read 68.2 on the hydrometer but wrote 63.5 in the ledger.
He poured 7.3 litres of water into 100 litres of spirit and measured 106.2 litres.
The cask filled to the bung at 63.5 percent.
A sealed sample bottle sat on the sill, yet the ledger showed no sample drawn.
rounds.chars: Rab; Inspector Sutherland (excise officer)
rounds.story: At 3:17 PM the spirit was 32°C, so the hydrometer's 68.2 reading corrected via the statutory temperature tables to the 63.5% ABV at 20°C recorded in the ledger. The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 cap cask filling at 63.5% ABV, and the 106.2 litres from mixing 7.3 litres of water with 100 litres follows the official contraction tables, while the sealed bottle was the excise officer's sample logged only in the Sample Register, not the production ledger.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Hamish, the stillman.
**Character 2:** Mr. Reid, the HM Customs & Excise officer.

**Story:** Hamish read the new-make spirit at 68.2% and recorded 63.5%, the cask-filling strength it would have after he reduced it. Adding 7.3 L of water to 100 L of spirit gave 106.2 L rather than 107.3 L because alcohol and water contract when mixed, which brought the cask to 63.5% right at the bung. The sealed bottle on the sill was Mr. Reid's official excise sample, drawn at full strength before the water went in. It was logged in the Crown's book rather than the distillery ledger, so the ledger showed no sample drawn.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 do not cap cask filling strength at 63.5% ABV (the real rule sets a minimum of 40% ABV for bottling, and 63.5% is a customary cask-filling strength rather than a statutory cap). Also, mixing 7.3 L of water into 100 L of spirit would give slightly less than 107.3 L because of volume contraction, but the "official contraction tables" and the Sample Register arrangement described are not an accurate account of the actual excise procedures.

opus.judge:
B

Story B ties every detail into one coherent sequence: reading, dilution with contraction, cask strength, and a sample logged in the Crown's book. Story A contradicts itself, since spirit already at 63.5% would fall below that once water was added, and its claimed 63.5% regulatory cap is invented.

A

Story A coherently links the 68.2 reading, the dilution with volume contraction, and the 63.5% cask strength, whereas in Story B the spirit is already 63.5% before water is added, so adding 7.3 litres could not leave the cask at 63.5%.

sol.judge:
B
It explains the ledger entry as the intended filling strength and the bottle as a separately logged excise sample, whereas A’s temperature correction would put the spirit at 63.5% before the water was added.

A
A more naturally connects the ledger entry to the intended filling strength and the sealed bottle to a separately logged excise sample, although its volumes imply about 64.2% ABV rather than 63.5%.

rounds.riddle:
Dawn breaks on the Paris picket line, where the union rep blocks the flour trucks.
He locks the ovens to the public, yet meticulously bakes exactly four hundred traditional loaves.
He leaves the ordinary dough safely in the freezer, but refuses to mix a single new batch.
The owner fumes at the closed doors, but cannot fire the man or dock his previous week's wages.
rounds.chars: Owner; Baker
rounds.story: The union rep meticulously bakes the already-mixed traditional dough because the 1993 "Décret Pain" strictly forbids freezing "pain de tradition" at any stage of production. He safely freezes the ordinary dough and avoids termination because deliberately letting the traditional dough overproof and rot would constitute "faute lourde" (gross misconduct) under French labor law, which would void his legal strike protections and allow the owner to dock his wages.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Marcel, a head baker and union rep
**Character 2:** Madame Duval, the bakery owner

**Story:** On the first morning of a legally declared national strike, Marcel blocks the flour deliveries and refuses to mix any new batch, which is a protected strike action under French law. He still bakes exactly four hundred traditional baguettes from the starter already on hand to feed the four hundred strikers on the picket line, and he leaves the ordinary dough frozen so none of Duval's stock spoils. Because of this, she can neither fire him nor touch the wages he already earned last week.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The 1993 Décret Pain (Décret n°93-1074) does reserve the "pain de tradition française" label to bread made without freezing at any stage of production, and French labor law does treat "faute lourde" (intent to harm the employer) as stripping a striker's usual protections, so the core mechanisms exist, though the riddle's specific scenario is embellished.

opus.judge:
A

Story A explains why only the traditional loaves had to be baked: French law bans freezing pain de tradition, so the already-mixed dough would otherwise rot and amount to gross misconduct. Story B's reason of feeding exactly 400 strikers is arbitrary and doesn't explain why the traditional dough was treated differently from the ordinary dough.

B
Story B explains why the traditional dough must be baked while the ordinary dough is frozen: French law forbids freezing *pain de tradition*. It also shows that avoiding deliberate spoilage keeps his strike protections intact, whereas Story A's "feeding the strikers" leaves the traditional/ordinary distinction unexplained.

sol.judge:
B
It explains the exact count with one loaf per striker and distinguishes protecting existing stock from refusing new work, without relying on A’s claim that strike misconduct could forfeit wages already earned.

A
It explains why he bakes exactly four hundred loaves without mixing new dough—one for each striker—while B explains why he bakes the traditional dough but not why he makes that exact number.

rounds.riddle: In a Paris shop on rue de Rivoli, the dough was mixed at ten, but at three the ovens stayed dark. The men outside refused to let them be lit, and at five they cheered though no loaf was baked. Why cheer at five if the bread was not ready?
rounds.chars: Émile; a journeyman baker (mitron)
rounds.story: Émile and the other mitrons were on the 1897 Paris bakery strike against night work, which is why they kept the ovens dark at three and cheered at five. The law they were enforcing defined night as 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. and allowed only the mixing of the dough during those hours, so ten was legal, three was illegal, and at five the ban lifted even though no loaf was baked yet.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Jules, a journeyman baker leading the strike.
**Character 2:** Monsieur Garnier, a master baker (occupation: bakery owner on rue de Rivoli).

**Story:** Garnier's apprentice mixed the dough at ten at night as usual, but when the ovens were due to be lit at three in the morning, Jules and his fellow striking journeymen blocked the doorway, refusing to let anyone work until the masters abolished the brutal all-night shifts. At five, with dawn approaching and not a single loaf in his window, Garnier gave in and signed their agreement, so the men cheered: the prize they had won was the end of night baking, not bread.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

There was no 1897 Paris law defining night as 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. for bakers; French bakers' night-work restrictions came later (the 1919 law banned work from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m.), and bakers' strikes and agitation over night work, though real, don't match this specific law or its hours.

opus.judge:
B
Story B explains every detail naturally: the dough was mixed as usual, the strikers blocked the ovens, and they cheered at five because the owner gave in, whereas Story A's claim that the men cheered merely because a legal ban lifted is a weaker motive.

B

Story B explains every time in the riddle through one rule: mixing was allowed at ten, baking was forbidden at three, and the ban lifted at five. Story A's capitulation at five is arbitrary and leaves the specific hours unexplained.

sol.judge:
A
The night-work rule explains all three times: mixing was allowed at ten, baking was barred at three, and five marked the end of the ban, not the arrival of fresh bread.

A
The owner’s concession gives the strikers a concrete victory to cheer at five, whereas the scheduled end of a ban doesn’t explain their celebration as naturally.

rounds.riddle:
He stirs the pot before sunrise,
his jaw is bare as the morning,
his master's beard is past his sash,
and he carries the master's sandals home.
rounds.chars: Takeshi; Master Gōzō (sumo stable master)
rounds.story: Takeshi is a junior rikishi at the Tokyo beya who cooks chanko-nabe for the sekitori and shaves daily, his rank too low to receive a sekitori's salary or silk apron; the Japan Sumo Association explicitly forbids active wrestlers from growing facial hair, so Master Gōzō's long beard openly identifies him as a retired tōshiyori elder who now runs the beya rather than a current competitor.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Ming, a beardless teenage novice.

**Character 2:** Master Huang, an old Taoist hermit-abbot who works as the mountain temple's herbalist and healer.

**Story:** Each day before sunrise, young Ming stirs the rice porridge for the temple, his jaw still smooth because novices may not grow a beard until they are ordained, while his master's long white beard has grown past his sash over sixty years of devotion. That morning Master Huang walked barefoot into the river shrine to pray, as the rite requires, so Ming humbly carried the old man's straw sandals home, as a disciple does for the teacher he hopes one day to become.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The core claim is shaky: sumo wrestlers are expected to be clean-shaven, but this is a matter of convention and the Sumo Association's grooming norms rather than an explicit beard ban. Also, stable masters (oyakata) are retired wrestlers who hold elder stock (toshiyori kabu), and they are typically clean-shaven too, so a long beard wouldn't be how an elder is identified. Several details also don't fit: junior rikishi do cook chanko, but the "silk apron" is the keshō-mawashi, which is a sekitori privilege.

opus.judge:
A
Story A accounts for every line, including why Ming carries the sandals home (the barefoot shrine rite), while Story B never explains the sandals and doesn't naturally fit a beard long enough to pass a sash.

B
Story B accounts for every line, including the sandals carried home after the barefoot river rite, while Story A never explains the sandals and depends on a stretch about the master's beard.

sol.judge:
A
It explains all four details, including why Ming carries his master’s sandals home, which Story B leaves unexplained.

B
It naturally explains all four details, including why the novice carries his master’s sandals home, which Story A leaves unexplained.

rounds.riddle:
I wept into a pine coffin and rolled past the king's red coat.
He raised a glass and missed the mourners' load.
When London sent his quill, my husband's hand refused—
the Spey still hums my name above the black rock.
rounds.chars: Helen Cumming; John Cumming (farmer)
rounds.story: Helen Cumming poured her husband's moonshine into a pine coffin, mounted it on a borrowed cart draped in black, and rolled it past the red-coated exciseman while he drank a glass at the farm door; under the Excise Act of 1823 the licensee became personally liable for the distillery duty, so when John Cumming—a tenant farmer—refused the quill and the legal burden, Helen signed Speyside's first distillery license herself, and her signature still hums in the Cardhu archive above the black rock by the river Spey.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Helen Cumming, a farmwife and illicit whisky distiller at Cardhu ("black rock" in Gaelic) on Speyside.

**Character 2:** A redcoat excise officer (occupation: exciseman/tax collector).

**Story:** Helen hid her illegal whisky in a pine coffin and wept over it in a fake funeral procession that rolled right past the redcoat exciseman, who had been plied with her hospitality and raised a glass instead of searching the mourners' load. When London later sent licensing papers to make the trade legal, her husband at first refused to sign, yet Helen's name lives on, still celebrated along the River Spey through Cardhu distillery above the black rock.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Excise Act of 1823 did exist and John Cumming took out Cardhu's license in 1824, but the key claim here is wrong: it was John, not Helen, who took the license, and the story that Helen signed instead of him because he refused is invented. Helen's real role was disguising illicit whisky and tricking excisemen, and the coffin cart episode and the signature "humming in the archive" are embellishment or fabrication, not the legal mechanism described.

opus.judge:
B
Story B explains every clue directly: the weeping fits a fake funeral, the exciseman raises a glass of her hospitality and misses the "mourners' load," the husband refuses to sign, and "black rock" is Cardhu's Gaelic meaning. Story A skips the weeping and leans on an invented legal-liability twist and an archive signature.

A

Story A naturally covers every line (the weeping over the coffin at a fake funeral, the toasting exciseman missing the mourners' load, the husband refusing London's papers, and her name living on at Cardhu), while Story B omits the weeping and mourners and leans on speculative legal and archival details.

sol.judge:
B
It explains the tears as part of the fake funeral and “black rock” as the meaning of Cardhu, without inventing a licensing signature to explain why Helen is remembered.

A
A directly explains the tears and mourners as part of a staged funeral, while B adds licensing details but never explains why Helen wept.

rounds.riddle:
Midland County, Texas, 2018—an oil rig drilling the Spraberry.
At 9,417 feet the bit suddenly sped up and the cuttings came up larger, yet the pit level never moved.
Jesse stopped the rotary and circulated for exactly 38 minutes, then looked at the pits.
Why did the pit level stay flat through all 38 minutes?
rounds.chars: Jesse; Renee (mudlogger)
rounds.story: The sudden faster bit and larger cuttings at 9,417 feet were a drilling break, meaning the bit had entered an overpressured Spraberry formation and Renee's d-exponent curve was dropping. The 38 minutes was the calculated mud lag time from bit to surface at that depth and pump rate—the standard bottoms-up circulation time—so any influx could not reach the shale shaker or raise the pit level until one full lag had passed, and Jesse stopped the rotary and circulated exactly that long to confirm the well was not flowing.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Jesse, the driller.
**Character 2:** Rosa, the mud logger.

**Story:** At 9,417 feet the bit broke into a softer, porous Spraberry sand, which is why it sped up and the cuttings came up larger. Jesse stopped rotating and circulated for 38 minutes, exactly the "bottoms-up" time Rosa had calculated, and the pits stayed flat because their mud weight was heavier than the formation's pore pressure, so no fluid could flow into the well and it was just a harmless drilling break, not a kick.
rounds.fact:
REAL
Drilling breaks (sudden ROP increase), the d-exponent trending down in overpressured zones, and lag time (bottoms-up time) as the delay before cuttings or influx reach surface are all genuine mudlogging and well-control concepts, and the Spraberry is a real Permian Basin formation (though it's typically underpressured to normally pressured, a minor detail).

opus.judge:
A

Story A explains the flat pits simply: the mud was heavier than the formation's pore pressure, so nothing flowed in. Story B wrongly claims an influx couldn't raise the pit level until bottoms-up, when in fact an influx gains pit volume immediately.

B

Story B explains the flat pits correctly: mud weight exceeded pore pressure, so no influx occurred. Story A wrongly claims an influx wouldn't raise pit level until bottoms-up, when in reality a pit gain shows immediately as formation fluid displaces mud.

sol.judge:
A
A softer sand explains the drilling break, and sufficient mud pressure prevented an influx; the 38 minutes was the bottoms-up time, not a delay before an influx could raise the pit level.

B
A softer formation explains the drilling break, and sufficient mud pressure explains why the pits stayed flat throughout the 38-minute bottoms-up circulation: an influx could raise the pit level before reaching the surface.

rounds.riddle:
I match your stride but wear no numbered chest,
A silent shadow putting you to test.
I break away before the red dirt bends,
Bound by a math that dictates where it ends.
rounds.chars: Kelvin; Samuel (pacemaker)
rounds.story: As a contracted pacemaker, Samuel was legally forbidden from racing Kelvin and faced a voided fee if his GPS watch logged him running even a meter past his strict 25-kilometer drop-out limit. Knowing the camp's steep red-dirt gorges caused GPS multipath errors that could artificially inflate his tracked distance, Samuel intentionally stopped his run 200 meters early at the curve to protect his paycheck.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Mara, an elite middle-distance runner chasing a record.

**Character 2:** Jonah, a professional pacemaker (a "rabbit") hired by the meet organizers.

**Story:** Jonah ran just ahead of Mara on the red track, matching her stride lap after lap. He wore no official race number because he was never meant to finish, and his pace sheet said he must peel away at exactly 800 meters, before the final bend, leaving her to chase the record alone.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Pacemakers (pacers) in marathons are commonly barred from competing and bound by contracts, and GPS multipath error in steep canyons can inflate tracked distance, so stopping short to avoid a contractual overrun is plausible.

opus.judge:
B
Story B covers every clue directly: a pacemaker with no race number, matching Mara's stride on a red track, peeling off at exactly 800 meters before the final bend as his pace sheet requires, while Story A relies on a strained GPS-error plot and never explains the missing numbered bib.

A
Story A naturally covers every clue: a pacemaker who matches the runner's stride, wears no race number, peels off before the final bend of the red track, and follows a pace sheet's math. Story B ignores the bib and stride details and stretches "math" into a convoluted GPS-error workaround.

sol.judge:
B
Jonah’s role as a pacemaker naturally explains why he matches Mara’s stride without a bib and why his pace sheet sends him off the red track at 800 meters, before the final bend.

A
Jonah matches Mara’s stride without a bib and peels off before the red track bends at the exact distance set by his pace sheet.

rounds.riddle:
On the fourth Thursday of March, the shutters of the Rue des Martyrs bakery stayed closed.  
For three dawns the workers sang, yet the ovens stayed cold after the city imposed a new flour levy.  
At noon the prefect delivered a note demanding a dozen loaves before nightfall.  
When the fire finally sparked, it glowed just half an hour before being snuffed.
rounds.chars: Henri; Claire (union rep)
rounds.story: Henri shut his ovens the moment the municipal council passed the March 1935 flour levy, a tax that prompted the three‑day strike Claire (union rep) had been rallying for, and the prefect’s noon decree that forced bakers to deliver at least a dozen loaves before nightfall to keep the levy in force. Because yeast left dormant for three days needs a minimum thirty‑minute warm‑up before it can leaven again—a little‑known rule of bakery science—Henri could only keep the fire alight for half an hour each sunrise, just enough to coax the dough back to life.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Madame Colette Rivaud, owner of the Rue des Martyrs bakery and leader of the bakers' strike.

**Character 2:** Prefect Augustin Delmas, the city's prefect, who imposed the new flour levy.

**Story:** For three dawns Colette's workers stood singing outside their cold ovens to protest Delmas's flour tax, until he sent a note demanding a dozen loaves for his own table by nightfall. Colette lit the oven just long enough to bake exactly twelve loaves, about half an hour. She delivered them to the prefect stamped with the words "Taxed Bread," then smothered the fire and kept the strike going.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The claimed "minimum thirty-minute warm-up rule" for yeast dormant three days isn't real bakery science, and the described levy, decree, and delivery requirement appear to be fabricated rather than documented legal mechanisms.

opus.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail directly: the singing strike, the prefect's note, and a half-hour fire used just to bake the twelve demanded loaves before resuming the strike. Story B depends on an invented yeast "rule," contradicts the cold ovens by having a fire lit each sunrise, and never really resolves the prefect's demand.

B
Story B explains every detail naturally (the singing strike, the noon note, and a half-hour fire just long enough to bake the twelve loaves before resuming the strike), while Story A leans on an invented "yeast rule" and contradicts itself by having the fire lit every sunrise even though the ovens stayed cold.

sol.judge:
A
The workers’ singing fits the strike, and baking exactly twelve loaves in one half-hour firing explains how the bakery met the prefect’s demand without ending the protest.

B
It explains why the workers sang outside the shuttered bakery for three dawns and why the noon demand prompted just one half-hour bake before the strike resumed.

rounds.riddle:
At rue des Martyrs the shutters stayed shut,
no fire was lit for seven days,
but on the eighth dawn one round loaf was sold
to a woman who paid in coins from '42.
rounds.chars: a baker; a woman in grey
rounds.story: The baker had joined the seven-day 1942 Paris bakers' strike against the German Occupation's bread decree, refusing to light his ovens in protest of the flour restrictions. The woman was sold the last round loaf because under the Occupation's "Décret Pain," bakeries were legally required to bake only round loaves — baguettes were forbidden — so the entire pre-strike inventory consisted of pain de rationnement.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Madame Lévy, an elderly woman who was hidden as a child during the 1942 Vel d'Hiv roundup.
**Character 2:** Samuel, a Jewish baker on rue des Martyrs, Paris.

**Story:** Samuel kept his shutters closed and his ovens cold for seven days while he sat shiva for his mother, who had sheltered Madame Lévy's family in 1942. On the eighth dawn he reopened and baked one round loaf, the mourners' symbol of life's cycle, and sold it to Madame Lévy, who paid with the very coins his mother had pressed into her hand the night she fled.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

There was no 1942 seven-day Paris bakers' strike against a German "Décret Pain," and baguettes were never banned in favor of round loaves; Vichy France did impose bread rationing and some regulations on flour and loaf types, but not this mechanism.

opus.judge:
A
Story A accounts for every detail naturally: the seven days of shiva explain the shut shutters and cold ovens, the round loaf marks the end of mourning, and the 1942 coins tie back to the past. Story B rests on invented historical events, never explains the eighth-dawn sale, and treats the coins as mere period currency.

B
Story B explains every detail: shiva accounts for the seven days with shutters shut and no fire, the round loaf is a mourning symbol, and the coins from '42 are the ones his mother gave the woman when she fled. Story A rests on an invented strike and decree, and it never explains why the woman paid with 1942 coins.

sol.judge:
A
Shiva explains the seven days of closed shutters and cold ovens, and the single round loaf on the eighth morning marks the end of mourning while the coins tie the sale to the baker’s mother and her act of kindness in 1942.

B
Shiva explains the seven-day closure and eighth-day reopening, while the round loaf marks mourning and the 1942 coins tie the woman to the baker’s mother.

rounds.riddle:
A year of Permian dust, one strike — the mud came back as gold;
He killed the well the very night it came in good and strong,
Then chased the last mail truck from town with a check for crude unsold —
Postmarked 11:59 on New Year's Eve, and the derrick went quiet all night long.
rounds.chars: Rex; Harlan (petroleum landman)
rounds.story: Harlan, the company's petroleum landman, knew the drilling lease's primary term expired at midnight on December 31, and the lease's shut-in royalty clause lets an operator keep the lease by tendering a payment in lieu of actual production — but only if the payment is tendered before the term expires, which is why he raced the mail truck so the check was postmarked at 11:59. He killed the well on purpose: with the clause payment holding the lease, he could leave the oil sealed in the ground until spring prices instead of selling into the winter glut, while roughneck Rex watched from the derrick floor, baffled that the first good strike was being welded shut.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Hank, a broke Permian Basin wildcatter whose drilling lease expired at midnight on New Year's Eve.

**Character 2:** Mrs. Delgado, a widowed rancher (the landowner) who held the mineral rights and was hoping the lease would lapse.

**Story:** After a year of dry holes, Hank's well hit oil on the lease's final day, but he had no pipeline or buyer, so he shut it in that night. Under the lease's shut-in royalty clause, a capped well still keeps the lease alive if the royalty payment goes out before the deadline, so he raced down the last mail truck to send Mrs. Delgado a check for oil he hadn't sold, postmarked 11:59 p.m., while the silent derrick kept his fortune safe in the ground.
rounds.fact:
REAL
Shut-in royalty clauses in oil and gas leases let an operator keep the lease alive past the primary term by paying a specified sum when a well capable of producing is shut in, though details like timely tender (some jurisdictions treat mailing as sufficient, others require receipt) and whether market-based shut-ins qualify vary by lease and state.

opus.judge:
B
Story B accounts for every detail most naturally: the year of dry holes, the strike on the lease's last day, shutting the well in for lack of a buyer, and mailing a shut-in royalty check before midnight. Story A leaves the "year of dust" unexplained and rests on a shakier price-waiting motive.

A
Story A explains every detail with one character: the year of dry holes, the shut-in because there was no buyer, and the shut-in royalty check for unsold crude mailed before the lease expired. Story B leaves the "year of Permian dust" unexplained, adds a speculative motive about spring prices, and splits the actions awkwardly between a landman and an onlooker.

sol.judge:
B
The lack of a pipeline or buyer explains why Hank immediately shut in a strong well, and the expiring lease explains why he raced to mail a royalty check despite selling no oil.

A
The lack of a pipeline or buyer naturally explains why Hank shut in a strong well without selling any oil, and the midnight lease deadline explains his race to mail the royalty check.

rounds.riddle:
On Iceland’s Westfjords the Björgvin drags a steel net of forty‑two knots.  
At 23:58 its engine coughs, then lies still for five heartbeats.  
When the net is hauled, a lone gull drops a stone onto the deck.  
The crew checks the ledger as the night deepens.
rounds.chars: Jón; Leifur (deckhand)
rounds.story: Jón and Leifur, aboard the trawler Björgvin, watch the 42‑knot net as the engine idles for the exact five‑minute window required to submit the catch report under Iceland’s Fisheries Act. After the pause they log the catch and steer toward the harbor before the midnight quota reset.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Gunnar, a drowned deckhand whose spirit now flies as a gull.

**Character 2:** Einar, skipper of the trawler *Björgvin* (occupation: fishing captain).

**Story:** Forty-two years ago at 23:58, Gunnar drowned when the *Björgvin*'s engine stalled. Each year since, Einar has tied one more knot into the net, and the old ledger records that Gunnar owes him a single stone for the five heartbeats he took to die. Tonight the engine coughs into the same silence, and the gull drops the stone on deck to settle the debt. Checking the ledger, the crew finds the final line, "paid in full," already written in Gunnar's hand.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Iceland's Fisheries Act doesn't require a trawler to idle its engine for a five-minute window to submit a catch report; catch reporting is done electronically through systems like Afladagbók and weighing at port, and the "42-knot net" and midnight quota reset are not real features of the regime.

opus.judge:
A
Story A accounts for every odd detail (the forty-two knots, the 23:58 stall, the five heartbeats, the gull's stone and the ledger), while Story B ignores the gull and stone entirely and turns "five heartbeats" into five minutes.

B
Story B accounts for every odd detail (the forty-two knots, the 23:58 stall, the five heartbeats, the gull's stone and the ledger) in one coherent tale, while Story A ignores the gull and stone and turns five heartbeats into five minutes.

sol.judge:
A
It ties the forty-two knots, the 23:58 stall, and the five heartbeats to Gunnar’s drowning, and explains the gull’s stone and the ledger as the settling of his debt.

B
B connects the forty-two knots, the 23:58 stall, the five heartbeats, the gull’s stone, and the ledger in one story, while A turns heartbeats into minutes and leaves the stone unexplained.

rounds.riddle:
The ovens ignite at three, yet the sun is high,  
The delegate taps the enriched, golden crown.  
The night-shift column in the ledger stays dry,  
The morning queue still receives their bread, unbound.
rounds.chars: Un Délégué Syndical; Un Compagnon Boulanger
rounds.story: During the June 1936 sit-down strikes, the CGT delegate occupied the bakery to enforce the Matignon Agreements but found the night ovens cold. The 1936 Collective Baking Agreement mandated a twelve-hour rest period after night work ending at 5 AM, making a 7 AM opening illegal for standard dough; the journeymen switched to baking enriched "Pain de Fantaisie" at 3 PM, legally classified as day-work pastry, to feed the queue without violating the rest clause or the strike's night stoppage.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Liv, the apprentice baker's delegate, who checks the loaves.
**Character 2:** Henrik, a master baker in Svalbard (occupation: baker).

**Story:** During the Arctic midnight sun, Henrik fires his ovens at 3 a.m. under a blazing sky, and he sends Liv to tap each egg-enriched, golden brioche crown to hear whether it is hollow and done. Because the sun never sets, the bakery's bookkeeper logs no "night shift" hours at all, yet the early queue still gets its loaves fresh and unwrapped as always.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Matignon Agreements (June 1936) were real and the sit-down strikes occurred, but there was no "1936 Collective Baking Agreement" setting a twelve-hour rest after night work ending at 5 AM, and no legal loophole classifying "pain de fantaisie" as day-work pastry. The night-baking ban in France dates to 1919 (the law banning night work in bakeries, with a 10 PM–4 AM window), so the described mechanism is fabricated.

opus.judge:
B
Story B explains every line naturally: the midnight sun puts a high sun at 3 a.m., the delegate taps the brioche crowns, no night shift is logged, and the queue gets unwrapped bread. Story A rests on convoluted legal reasoning and never explains the crown-tapping.

B
Story B accounts for every detail more naturally: the union delegate, the enriched "fantaisie" bread, ovens lit at 3 PM under a high sun, and an empty night-shift column caused by the strike's legal rules, whereas Story A must stretch to explain why the 3 a.m. hours would not count as night shift.

sol.judge:
A
The day-work classification makes the enriched bread, the 3 p.m. bake, and the blank night-shift ledger part of one workaround that keeps the morning queue supplied.

A
The midnight sun explains daylight at 3 a.m. and the blank night-shift column, while Liv’s tap tests the golden brioche and the early bake supplies the morning queue with unwrapped bread.

rounds.riddle:
As the bridal chorus hummed a Malayalam lullaby near ten,
the one with the bow and hollow wood snapped a string with a sharp crack, killing the note.
The bride’s father began his speech in a whisper,
while the groom’s uncle in khaki nodded.
rounds.chars: Suresh (Police Sub-Inspector); Reji (Violinist)
rounds.story: A 10 PM noise curfew forced the reception into sudden silence. Under Kerala’s entertainer permit rules, any note past the deadline triggers immediate confiscation of the instrument, so Reji broke the string to guarantee no sound lingered past the hour.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Meera, the wedding violinist.

**Character 2 (with occupation):** Uncle Raghavan, the groom's uncle and an on-duty police sub-inspector (hence the khaki), responsible for enforcing Kerala's 10 p.m. noise curfew.

**Story:** As the clock neared ten and the chorus's Malayalam lullaby finally lulled the bride's newborn nephew to sleep, Meera deliberately snapped a violin string so the music would end before the curfew without an awkward announcement. The bride's father, mindful of both the sleeping baby and the law, gave his toast in a whisper, and Uncle Raghavan nodded his approval that the wedding was now legally and peacefully quiet.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Kerala does enforce a 10 PM loudspeaker/noise curfew under national Noise Pollution Rules, but those rules target amplified sound and have no "entertainer permit" provision that confiscates an instrument for a single note past the deadline, so the confiscation mechanism is fabricated.

opus.judge:
A
Story A accounts for every detail, including the lullaby, the snapped string, the whispered speech, and the khaki-clad uncle's nod, while Story B ignores the lullaby and the whisper and rests on an invented confiscation rule.

B

Story B accounts for every detail, including why a lullaby was sung, why the father whispered, and why the khaki-clad uncle approved, while Story A relies on an invented permit rule and leaves the lullaby unexplained.

sol.judge:
A
The sleeping baby explains both the lullaby and the father’s whisper, while the curfew explains why the violinist stopped playing and the uncle in khaki nodded his approval.

B
It connects the lullaby and whispered speech to the sleeping baby, explains the khaki-clad uncle’s nod, and ties the snapped string to the approaching curfew without inventing an immediate-confiscation rule.

rounds.riddle:
A dozen years in oak, the butt was sound,
one teaspoon, not its own, the only wound.
No padlock broke, no angel claimed a dram,
yet the cask left bond without its name or stamp.
rounds.chars: Ewan; Morag, the cooper
rounds.story: Ewan had brokered the twelve-year-old butt from the distillery, but Morag, the cooper, drew one teaspoon of Glenfarclas and slipped it through the bung before the cask left bond, because any cask containing spirit from more than one distillery is classified under the Scotch Whisky Regulations as a Blended Malt, stripping it of the right to bear the original still's name. When the independent laboratory confirmed the trace second distillery in the profile, Ewan's buyer dropped the price by sixty percent, even though the cask held five hundred litres of the same whisky he had tasted when he bought it.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Mrs. Isla Grant, owner of a famous single-malt distillery.

**Character 2:** Rory Dunn, an independent bottler (cask broker) buying her whisky.

**Story:** When Isla sold Rory a sound twelve-year-old sherry butt, her contract forbade him from using her distillery's prized name, so before it left bond her warehouseman "teaspooned" it with a single spoonful of malt from another distillery. Nothing was stolen or lost to evaporation, but that one foreign teaspoon legally turned the single malt into an anonymous blended malt, and it shipped out with no name or distillery stamp at all.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, a Blended Malt is a blend of single malts from more than one distillery, but a cask is not reclassified by a teaspoon of foreign spirit, and no lab-based "trace" test exists that would reliably detect this. The scenario also has problems on bond and labeling: adding spirit from another distillery would breach bonded warehouse controls, and the "Single Malt" label requires a single distillery, so the label would indeed be lost, but the detectability and the "stripped of the still's name" mechanism are misdescribed.

opus.judge:
B

Story B gives a natural motive (the distillery protecting its name) and explicitly covers each line of the riddle: a sound cask, one foreign teaspoon, nothing stolen or evaporated, and shipping out unnamed and unstamped, whereas Story A leaves the cooper's motive unexplained and adds a price-drop subplot the riddle never mentions.

A
Story A explains every line naturally, including the motive for the foreign teaspoon, while Story B leaves the cooper's motive unexplained and adds an irrelevant price-drop subplot.

sol.judge:
B
It naturally explains the foreign teaspoon as a deliberate way to protect the distillery’s name, while accounting for the intact cask, the absence of whisky loss, and the missing name and stamp.

A
It explains the foreign teaspoon as a deliberate way to protect the distillery’s name and accounts for the cask leaving bond unmarked without any theft or evaporation.

rounds.riddle:
At 5:12 AM, a second pair of scissors clicks.
The yokozuna waits while jonokuchi are styled first.
The stablemaster's wife seals two envelopes, not one.
An apprentice brushes hair from a sandanme shoulder.
rounds.chars: The stablemaster's wife; The visiting 1st-class tokoyama (sumo hairdresser)
rounds.story: The Sumo Association mandates that only a 1st-class tokoyama may style a yokozuna's oicho-mage, forcing the stable's regular 2nd-class hairdresser to finish all lower-ranked wrestlers before the visiting specialist arrives for the grand champion. The stablemaster's wife pays the visiting tokoyama a daily cash fee in a separate envelope from the regular's monthly retainer, explaining the two payments and the early start needed to clear the junior wrestlers first.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Takeshi, a sandanme wrestler retiring quietly before dawn.
**Character 2:** Old Sato, the stable's senior *tokoyama* (sumo hairdresser), who is training his replacement.

**Story:** At 5:12 AM, Sato's apprentice picked up his own scissors for the first time to snip Takeshi's topknot in a private retirement cut, then brushed the fallen hair from his shoulder, while the yokozuna waited because the novice had to practice on the jonokuchi first. The stablemaster's wife sealed two envelopes: one a farewell gift for Takeshi, and one the apprentice's first wages as a true tokoyama.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Tokoyama are ranked and sekitori wrestlers get the oicho-mage, but there is no Sumo Association rule that only a 1st-class tokoyama may style a yokozuna's hair, nor a system of visiting specialists paid by the stablemaster's wife in separate daily envelopes.

opus.judge:
A

Story A accounts for every clue: the apprentice's first scissors, the yokozuna waiting during jonokuchi practice, the two envelopes, and the hair brushed from a sandanme shoulder. Story B leaves the apprentice and the sandanme shoulder unexplained.

B
Story B accounts for every clue: the apprentice's first scissors, the brushed hair on the sandanme shoulder, the yokozuna's wait, and both envelopes. Story A never explains the apprentice or the sandanme detail.

sol.judge:
A
A ties the second scissors and the hair on the sandanme wrestler’s shoulder to the apprentice’s retirement cut, while also explaining why the juniors go first and who gets each envelope.

B
B ties the second scissors to the apprentice and the hair on the sandanme wrestler’s shoulder to his retirement cut, while also explaining the juniors’ priority and the two envelopes.

rounds.riddle:
We launched the whisper that hunts for screams.
The cook’s knife missed the onion and rang on the steel.
In the hush that followed, we heard our own doom swimming back.
Only the log reveals the missing ingredient in the recipe.
rounds.chars: Hein; the Cook
rounds.story: Hein, the hydrophone operator, was logging all sounds during the Zaunkönig run, and the exact second he noted the knife’s clang matched the moment the torpedo swung around; the acoustic homing mechanism locked onto that sound, and the war diary’s time stamps confirmed the missing ingredient was the silence the cook’s recipe required.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The Captain of a WWII-era submarine.
**Character 2:** Petey, the submarine's galley cook.

**Story:** The Captain fired an acoustic homing torpedo, a quiet "whisper" built to hunt the loudest noise in the sea, and in that silent-running hush Petey's knife slipped off an onion and clanged against the steel galley counter. The torpedo locked onto the new sound and turned back toward its own boat, and only the recovered patrol log reveals the missing ingredient in the "recipe" for silent running: Petey was never told the order to keep absolute quiet.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The German Zaunkönig (G7es T5) was a real acoustic homing torpedo that locked onto the propeller noise of ships, and the Allies' Foxer noisemaker decoys exploited that same mechanism, so a loud sound could plausibly divert it. The riddle's story is embellished (a knife clang is an odd trigger, and the T5 homed on cavitation and propeller noise), but the acoustic-homing principle and hydrophone logging are genuine.

opus.judge:
A

Story A ties every line together: a hydrophone operator hears the torpedo "swimming back," and his time-stamped sound log matching the knife's clang to the torpedo's turn is exactly what "only the log reveals" implies. Story B's claim that a patrol log would record the cook never being told to keep quiet is more of a stretch.

B
Story B ties every line together: the hydrophone operator's sound log explains how they "heard" their doom returning, and its time stamps explain how "only the log" exposes silence as the missing ingredient, whereas Story A's claim that a patrol log records Petey never being told is a stretch.

sol.judge:
B
B makes the “missing ingredient” a specific omission revealed by the log—the cook was never given the order to keep quiet—rather than simply the silence whose absence the clang already makes obvious.

A
A makes the missing ingredient a specific omission—the cook never received the silent-running order—whereas B’s timestamps only confirm when the clang occurred.

rounds.riddle:
The codend breaks the surface, heavy with silver, but the winch falls dead halfway up.  
The wheelhouse door opens; the Old Man checks his watch—eighteen minutes since the doors kissed bottom—then nods.  
On the factory deck, the Baader sits silent, a single red fault light blinking over a static conveyor.  
"Twenty minutes," the winchman grunts, lighting a cigarette. "Or the whole haul goes white."
rounds.chars: The Old Man; The Mate (Deck Officer)
rounds.story: The trawler was a freezer vessel targeting "Super Prime" cod, a grade demanding every fish be bled and gutted within twenty minutes of leaving the water to prevent gaping and secure the sashimi premium. Because their processor's contract enforced lot integrity—downgrading the *entire* haul to standard white-flesh price if even one fish missed the window—the Mate halted the winch to cap the batch at the volume the jammed Baader could process before the eighteen-minute mark expired.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The Old Man, the trawler's skipper.

**Character 2:** Sven, the factory-deck engineer who keeps the Baader filleting machine running.

**Story:** The Baader jammed just as the skipper realized his short eighteen-minute tow had filled the net with prime fish, so he signaled the winchman to deliberately "kill" the winch and leave the codend hanging half-submerged, keeping the catch alive and cold in the sea. Everyone now waits on Sven: if he can't clear the red fault in twenty minutes, the fish will die, their eyes and flesh will cloud white, and the whole haul will be downgraded to fishmeal instead of fillets.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Real cod handling does stress prompt bleeding and gutting for quality, and Baader makes real fish-processing machines. However, I know of no "Super Prime" cod grade with a twenty-minute gut-by window, no sashimi premium for cod, and no contract that downgrades an entire haul because one fish misses the window. Cod quality is judged on bleeding, chilling and handling, not on a lot-wide timed cutoff like this.

opus.judge:
A

Story A coherently explains the deliberate winch stop (keeping the short-towed, still-living catch cold in the sea), the 20-minute deadline to fix the jammed Baader, and "goes white" as spoilage. Story B muddles its timing and has a jammed machine somehow processing fish.

B
Story B coherently explains the deliberate winch stop (keeping the catch alive in the water), the skipper's nod, the jammed Baader, and the twenty-minute deadline, whereas Story A contradicts itself by relying on a jammed machine to process fish.

sol.judge:
A
The skipper’s nod makes sense as a signal to keep the catch partly submerged while the Baader is down, whereas B has the crew timing processing from when the trawl doors hit bottom rather than when the fish leave the water.

B
It connects the eighteen-minute tow, the skipper’s nod, and the stalled winch by making the half-submerged net a way to keep the catch alive while the crew clears the Baader jam.

rounds.riddle:
At sunrise, a boat from Tampico arrived with a hold of oranges.
The captain swept an arm across the empty horizon.
The rig boss just pointed up at the Stars and Stripes.
Not a single piece of fruit was swung aboard.
rounds.chars: Captain; Rig Boss (Company Man)
rounds.story: The rig boss knew the Jones Act treats a fixed offshore rig as a U.S. coastwise point, banning a foreign-flagged ship from carrying any merchandise directly from a foreign port. The captain’s appeal to international waters failed because U.S. law extends to structures on the Outer Continental Shelf, making even a crate of oranges an illegal coastwise shipment.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Captain Ramírez, a Mexican supply-boat skipper.
**Character 2:** Hank, an offshore oil-rig boss (platform superintendent) on a U.S. Gulf of Mexico rig.

**Story:** Ramírez sailed out from Tampico with a cheap load of Mexican oranges for the rig's galley, sweeping his arm across the empty sea to say, "Who's out here to check?" Hank just pointed at the American flag, because the rig is U.S. jurisdiction and Mexican citrus is banned there under fruit-fly quarantine rules, so not one orange came aboard.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The Jones Act (46 U.S.C. 55102) restricts carriage of merchandise between U.S. points to U.S.-built, -owned, and -crewed vessels, and via the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, fixed OCS installations are treated as U.S. points. But a shipment coming directly from a foreign port to a rig isn't coastwise transport, so the claim that a foreign ship carrying oranges directly from a foreign port is banned is materially wrong (the issue arises mainly when cargo is picked up at a U.S. point or transshipped).

opus.judge:
B

Story B explains the arm sweep ("who's out here to check?"), the flag (U.S. jurisdiction), and why oranges specifically were refused (fruit-fly quarantine on Mexican citrus), whereas Story A rests on a shaky Jones Act claim that doesn't depend on the cargo being fruit.

A

Story A naturally explains the captain's "who's checking?" gesture and the flag-pointing as U.S. jurisdiction enforcing a real fruit-fly quarantine on Mexican citrus, while Story B misapplies the Jones Act, which governs shipments between two U.S. points, not from a foreign port.

sol.judge:
B
The quarantine explains why the oranges specifically were refused, while the flag answers the captain’s suggestion that no one was around to enforce U.S. rules.

A
The citrus quarantine explains why the oranges mattered and why the U.S. flag answered the captain’s gesture, whereas the Jones Act does not generally bar direct shipments from foreign ports.

rounds.riddle: Paris, August 1978: every shop on the rue is shuttered in a strike against a foe who never touches dough, yet one oven glows all night, and its owner leads the dawn picket with flour still on his sleeves, pressing warm loaves into comrades' hands while not one coin crosses his counter, and on his window hangs the list the law demands — every name on it, but his, is dark.
rounds.chars: Étienne Roux, picket leader; Marcel Deschamps (baker)
rounds.story: Étienne Roux called the street's bakers out in August 1978 against the Barre government's plan to end bread's long-standing VAT exemption, but Marcel Deschamps could not close with them, because the Paris prefecture's staggered-closure arrêté — the rule meant to guarantee every neighborhood always has bread — designated his shop as the one that must stay lit on their block that week, so he baked all night as the law required and still reached the barricades by dawn to march at the head of Étienne's picket with flour on his sleeves. Bound by that same prefectural rule to keep his oven hot and his window notice accurate, Marcel hung the legally required list that morning showing every neighboring bakery dark but his own, and, refusing to earn a single franc from a strike he marched in, he handed his warm baguettes to the pickets for free.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Raymond Barre, the French Prime Minister who controlled bread prices and never touched dough.

**Character 2:** Monsieur Lefèvre, a Paris baker (boulanger).

**Story:** In August 1978, Paris bakers struck against the state's fixed bread prices, but Lefèvre's name sat alone, still lit, on the legally required summer rota of bakeries obliged to stay open, so his oven had to burn all night. To keep faith with his comrades without breaking the strike, he baked as the law demanded but sold nothing, marching at dawn and handing out his loaves free so that not one franc reached Barre's price-fixed counter.
rounds.fact:
REAL

France did have prefectural arrêtés requiring staggered bakery closures (congés annuels rotation) so that each neighborhood always had a bakery open, and bakers had to post notices of which shops were open. The 1978 Barre-era context is also plausible, since bread prices were liberalized in 1978 and VAT debates existed, though the specific strike is a fictional detail.

opus.judge:
B

Story B explains every clue tightly: Barre as the foe who never touches dough, the legally required summer rota with only the baker's name lit, and the oven burning all night by law, with free loaves keeping his coins off the price-fixed counter.

A

Story A ties every detail together tightly (the lone lit name on the legal rota, the all-night oven, the free loaves so no coin crosses the counter) without B's extra character, whose role as picket leader conflicts with the baker leading the picket.

sol.judge:
A
It explains why the baker had to keep his oven lit, why his name alone was marked open on the required window list, and how he still led the dawn picket without taking a coin.

A
A makes the baker himself the dawn picket leader and ties his lone lit name to the mandatory summer rota, while the price-control dispute explains why he gives away the bread rather than selling it.

rounds.riddle:
Red dust caked my soles after the morning’s forty-two,
An acacia held a clear bag at noon for no bleeding goat,
The stranger in sunglasses filmed the drip from the branch,
And the man in white will never stamp another team ledger.
rounds.chars: Kiptoo; Ochieng (camp medic)
rounds.story: Kiptoo had just finished the camp’s weekly forty-two-kilometre morning run through the Rift Valley red dirt when Ochieng, the camp medic, spiked a one-litre bag of saline into his arm from an acacia branch to hasten recovery. An unannounced Athletics Integrity Unit officer filmed the scene because WADA’s Prohibited List treats any intravenous infusion over one hundred millilitres within a twelve-hour window as a prohibited method unless the athlete holds a Therapeutic Use Exemption, and the AIU’s lesser-known “administration of a prohibited method” clause sanctions support personnel who deliver it, which is why Ochieng was stripped of his team travel credentials while Kiptoo—having received only seventy millilitres—was cleared to line up in Rotterdam.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** A Kenyan marathon runner (the narrator).

**Character 2:** The team doctor (the man in white coat).

**Story:** After a 42-km training marathon on red-dirt roads, the doctor hung an IV bag from an acacia branch at noon to give me a banned blood-boosting infusion, not to treat any slaughtered goat. An undercover journalist in sunglasses filmed the drip, and the footage got the doctor banned for life from signing off on any team's medical records again.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

WADA's Prohibited Method M2 does ban intravenous infusions over 100 mL per 12 hours (except for legitimate medical treatment, hospital admission, or with a TUE), but the answer is internally inconsistent: it says Kiptoo received a one-litre bag, then claims he got only seventy millilitres, and the sanction against support personnel is also described loosely rather than through a distinct "lesser-known clause."

opus.judge:
A
Story A ties every clue together cleanly: the 42-km run, the IV bag that wasn't for a goat, the filming stranger, and the white-coated doctor's lifetime ban from signing records. Story B contradicts itself (a one-litre bag but only seventy millilitres received), never explains the "man in white," and gives only a credential loss rather than a permanent end.

B
Story B explains every line simply (the 42 km run, the IV bag on the acacia, the journalist filming, and the doctor's lifetime ban), while Story A contradicts itself with a one-litre bag of which only seventy millilitres was given and loosely turns "never stamp another team ledger" into losing travel credentials.

sol.judge:
A
It directly explains the sunglasses as an undercover disguise and the final line as a lifetime ban, whereas B leaves the sunglasses unexplained and substitutes a loss of travel credentials.

B
It explicitly explains the sunglasses and the permanent ban, while A undermines its own explanation by saying the runner received less than the prohibited volume.

rounds.riddle:
At three‑fifteen the copper beast lets out a sigh,  
While a wooden bung is lifted from the fourth cask,  
The bookkeeper writes “no cork” as if it mattered,  
And the night watch knows the law demands a count at midnight.
rounds.chars: Finlay; Mona (Distillery Tax Officer)
rounds.story: At precisely 3:15 p.m., the copper pot still sighs as it finishes its final run, and Finlay lifts the wooden bung from cask 4, noting “no cork” in the ledger because the Scotch Whisky Regulations require any wood‑bunged cask to be flagged for excise accounting. Mona, the distillery’s tax officer, then carries out the compulsory midnight stock‑take—a lesser‑known clause of HMRC’s Excise Notice 3 that triggers a night‑audit of every cask recorded as “no cork”.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Eli, the distillery's night watchman.
**Character 2:** Mr. Haskett, an excise officer (the "gauger") who must count and seal every cask at midnight by law.

**Story:** Each night at three-fifteen, when the copper still's pressure valve sighs loudly enough to cover any sound, Eli pulls the wooden bung from the fourth cask, which he left uncorked after Haskett's midnight count, and siphons off whiskey to sell untaxed. The bookkeeper dutifully logs "no cork" on that cask every morning, never realizing that this one detail is the only record of the theft, since Haskett's legal count happens hours before the barrel is ever touched.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
No UK rule requires flagging wood-bunged casks as "no cork" for excise accounting, and HMRC's Excise Notice 3 (spirit duty) contains no clause mandating a midnight stock-take or night-audit triggered by such a ledger entry.

opus.judge:
A
Story A ties every detail into one coherent scheme: the still's sigh masks the theft, the midnight count happens before the 3:15 siphoning, and "no cork" becomes the only trace of it, while Story B relies on invented regulations and explains nothing odd.

B
Story B ties every detail into one coherent theft: the still's sigh masks the sound, the "no cork" note becomes the only trace of the crime, and the midnight count explains the timing gap. Story A leans on invented regulations and leaves the details only loosely linked.

sol.judge:
A
The still’s sigh masks the watchman’s theft after the midnight count, and “no cork” becomes an unwitting clue rather than a contrived regulatory flag.

A
A ties the sigh, the removal of the fourth cask’s bung, the ledger entry, and the midnight count into one excise procedure, whereas B has Eli pull a bung from a cask he supposedly already left uncorked.

rounds.riddle:
Four times the trawl came up forlorn,  
The fifth a single silver scale.  
The captain cursed the clock that morn,  
And let the severed cable sail.
rounds.chars: Einar; Captain Ólafur
rounds.story: Einar saw the salmon scale snagged in the mesh—proof a salmon had escaped, a species strictly forbidden to possess at sea under Icelandic law. Because even a single scale triggers a mandatory gear inspection and risks license suspension, Captain Ólafur cursed the approaching dock-time and cut the warp to sink the evidence.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** A mermaid.

**Character 2:** A fishing-boat captain who had fallen in love with her.

**Story:** The mermaid could stay with the captain only until sunrise, and when dawn came she slipped back into the sea. He dragged the trawl five times to find her, but the last haul held only one of her silver scales, so he cursed the clock that had ended their night and cut the net loose so it could never catch her.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Icelandic law doesn't forbid possessing salmon at sea in this way (salmon fishing at sea is banned in Iceland, but a single scale in a net doesn't trigger a mandatory gear inspection or license suspension), so the central mechanism is fabricated.

opus.judge:
B
Story B accounts for every detail naturally: the empty hauls are his search for her, the single scale is all she left, the clock is the dawn that took her, and he cuts the cable so the net can never catch her, whereas Story A relies on an invented law and a strained reading of "clock" as dock-time.

A
Story A accounts for the empty hauls (searching for her), the single silver scale (all that remained of her), the cursed clock (sunrise ending their night), and the cut cable (so the net could never catch her), while Story B relies on a contrived legal premise, leaves the four empty hauls unexplained, and stretches "clock" to mean dock-time.

sol.judge:
B
The mermaid’s dawn departure explains the four empty hauls, the lone silver scale, and why the captain curses the time and cuts the cable to keep the net from ever catching her.

A
The mermaid’s departure at sunrise explains the five search hauls, the lone silver scale, the captain’s curse at the clock, and his decision to cut the cable so the net could never catch her.

rounds.riddle:
He grips the blackened thread to bind the heavy yellow sun,
But the water basin swears the sacred pendant is undone.
A needle pricks the crest to let a single phantom flee,
The liquid yields its truth, and they are wed at half past three.
rounds.chars: The Groom; The Goldsmith
rounds.story: Because the traditional Kerala Minnu pendant is constructed with a hollow brass core to maximize its visual size, the goldsmith's hydrostatic purity test initially failed as the trapped air artificially increased the object's buoyancy, making the 22-karat shell appear to be a lesser alloy. To correct this anomaly in Archimedes' principle of water displacement, the goldsmith pricked a microscopic vent hole in the pendant's crest to release the trapped air bubble, allowing the liquid to accurately measure the true volume of the gold so the groom could proceed with the wedding at the astrologically chosen time of 3:30.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Tomas, a nervous groom.
**Character 2:** Mrs. Adler, a goldsmith.

**Story:** On his wedding morning, Tomas suspended his grandmother's heavy gold pendant from a blackened thread into Mrs. Adler's water basin, and the displacement test suggested it was too light to be real gold. Mrs. Adler spotted a tiny air bubble trapped inside the hollow crest, pricked it free with a needle, and re-weighed it; the water proved the gold genuine, and Tomas wore it proudly at his 3:30 wedding.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Kerala minnu is a real wedding pendant, but it is not made with a hollow brass core under a 22-karat shell, and the "air bubble fix" doesn't fit how hydrostatic testing works. Trapped air would make the object displace more water and look less dense, so the mechanism is partly plausible. However, goldsmiths test purity with touchstones, acid, or fire assay rather than a vented-pendant water test, and a hollow brass-core piece would not be a 22-karat gold item.

opus.judge:
A
Story A explains every clue (thread, gold pendant, failed water test, needle releasing the trapped air, 3:30 wedding) in a consistent way, whereas Story B's brass core contradicts its claim that the water test then proved the pendant genuine gold.

B

Story B accounts for every clue coherently: the blackened thread, the failed water test, the needle releasing the trapped "phantom" bubble, and the 3:30 wedding. Story A never mentions the thread, and its brass core muddles the purity logic.

sol.judge:
A
A accounts for the blackened thread and the single trapped bubble without B’s questionable claim that a displacement test can isolate the gold content of a brass-cored pendant.

B
It accounts for the blackened thread, the misleading water test, the needle releasing a single bubble, and the 3:30 wedding without introducing a brass core that would complicate the purity reading.

rounds.riddle:
Before our 35k, a man at the gate clicked a silver pen.  
His watch chirped twice, and he was gone before the slowest runner rounded the acacia.  
I asked no one; no one asked me.  
The second chirp still hangs in the air.
rounds.chars: The runner; a Doping Control Officer
rounds.story: The man was a Doping Control Officer conducting a no‑notice test during my mandated 60‑minute whereabouts window. The watch’s two chirps marked the window’s start and end, and when it closed before I returned, regulation forced him to record a missed test and leave immediately.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The narrator, an elite distance runner.
**Character 2:** A team "physician" who secretly works as a doping supplier.

**Story:** At the start gate of a 35k on an acacia-lined course, the doctor pressed a silver injector pen (disguised as a pen) into the narrator's arm, and his watch chirped twice: once to mark the dose, once to confirm the drug would clear before testing. He slipped away before the slowest runner even reached the acacia, and the narrator kept the unspoken pact of silence, though the memory of that second chirp, the moment of becoming a cheat, still haunts every victory.
rounds.fact:
REAL

WADA's whereabouts rules require athletes in the testing pool to name a daily 60-minute window and be available for no-advance-notice testing, and a Doping Control Officer who cannot find the athlete in that window records a "missed test" (an unsuccessful attempt) and leaves after making a reasonable effort. The detail that the officer must leave immediately is a mild embellishment, since the rules require the DCO to stay for a time within the window, and the watch chirps are just narrative color.

opus.judge:
B

Story B accounts for every detail: the "pen" is a clicking injector, the chirps mark dose and clearance, the hasty exit, the mutual silence of a secret pact, and the haunting guilt. Story A strains, since a whereabouts test makes little sense when the runner is plainly present at a race.

A

Story A accounts for every detail: the silver pen as a disguised injector, the two chirps, the doctor's quick exit, the mutual silence of a shared secret, and the lingering guilt. Story B leaves the pen and the silence unexplained, and it contradicts the narrator being present to witness the scene.

sol.judge:
B
The injector pen and shared silence give the second chirp a lasting emotional weight that the missed-test explanation leaves largely unexplained.

A
The clicked pen, the man’s quick departure, and the mutual silence fit a covert exchange, while the second chirp gives the narrator a specific moment to feel haunted by.

rounds.riddle:
At 4:17 the father checks the well-water's degree
Seven rice grains weigh the gold while the thaali turns east
The plantain leaf stays folded past the second conch's call
The groom's sister holds a brass key that fits no door at all
rounds.chars: The bride's father; the goldsmith
rounds.story: The 4:17 timing and thermometer reveal the kanyadaanam occurs at the true muhurtham shifted 17 minutes early by the Kollavarsham calendar's pre-leap-year intercalation drift, while the well water must hit exactly 24°C for the ritual pour. The seven rice grains weigh the gold because the Travancore Goldsmiths' Guild regulation mandates the Nel-Kasu purity test — exactly seven standardized paddy grains counterbalancing the thaali — and this verification must coincide with the true muhurtham, explaining why the thaali faces east toward the guild's founding shrine during the weighing.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Lakshmi, the groom's sister.
**Character 2:** Raghavan, the family's temple astrologer (occupation: astrologer-priest).

**Story:** Raghavan fixed the dawn muhurta at 4:17 and ordered every rite to wait for its signs: the well-water warming by a set degree, the gold thaali balanced against seven rice grains and turned east, and the plantain leaves kept folded so no one ate before the tying. Lakshmi's brass key fits no door because it opens her late mother's locked jewel-trunk, which by custom she must hand to the bride only after the second conch sounds and the thaali is tied, making the bride the new keeper of the house.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Kanyadaanam and the Kollavarsham calendar are real, but the "pre-leap-year intercalation drift" shifting the muhurtham by 17 minutes, the 24°C well-water requirement, and a Travancore Goldsmiths' Guild "Nel-Kasu" regulation that weighs the thaali against seven paddy grains are fabricated.

opus.judge:
A
Story A accounts for every line, including the folded plantain leaf and the doorless brass key, while Story B skips those details entirely and leans on invented, far-fetched calendar and guild rules.

B
Story B accounts for all four details, including the folded plantain leaf and the brass key that fits no door, while Story A never explains the leaf or the key and relies on invented calendar drift and guild regulations.

sol.judge:
A
It ties the timing, water check, and gold weighing to a single wedding ritual and explains the folded leaf, second conch, and sister’s trunk key, which B leaves unaddressed.

B
It ties the water check, seven-grain weighing, and eastward turn to the 4:17 wedding rite while also explaining the folded leaf and the sister’s trunk key, which A leaves unaddressed.

rounds.riddle:
The copper neck runs clear at sixty-two,  
The locked glass box waits, the officer overdue.  
Steam climbs, the lever's ready — but the key stays gone,  
One cut sits trapped until the bell rings on.
rounds.chars: The stillman; the excise officer
rounds.story: The spirit safe showed the heart cut flowing bright at 62% ABV, but the excise officer held the only key to swing the divider from feints to spirit receiver. When his lunch ran long, the falling still strength pushed the valuable middle cut into the low wines charger, condemning a week's malt to re-distillation.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Angus, the stillman at a Scotch whisky distillery.

**Character 2:** Mr. Reid, the excise officer who holds the only key to the distillery's padlocked brass-and-glass spirit safe.

**Story:** As steam climbed through the still's copper swan neck, Angus watched the new spirit run clear at 62% strength, ready to throw the lever and send the precious middle cut to the receiver. But the safe's diverting lever had been locked under seal, and Mr. Reid was late, so the cut stayed trapped in the glass box until the gate bell rang to announce his arrival with the key.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
In Scotch whisky distilling, the spirit safe was locked by the excise officer, but the stillman operates the cut by swinging the brass divider/handwheel to direct flow to the spirit receiver, feints, or foreshots, and an officer's absence would not force the heart cut into the low wines charger (which is a separate pre-distillation vessel), so the described mechanism is materially wrong.

opus.judge:
A

Story A covers every clue, including the cut staying trapped in the locked safe until the bell announces the officer's arrival, while Story B never mentions a bell and has the cut diverted rather than held.

B
Story B explains every element, including the copper swan neck, the climbing steam, the ready lever, the locked glass safe, the overdue officer and the bell announcing his arrival, while Story A leaves out the bell and steam and has the cut diverted rather than held "until the bell rings."

sol.judge:
A
It explains the steam, the locked lever, and the missing key, and gives the bell a clear role: announcing the officer’s arrival.

B
It accounts for the locked lever, the missing key, and the bell that announces the officer’s arrival, while A sends the cut elsewhere and leaves the bell unexplained.

rounds.riddle:
The derrickhand wraps the vent line in heat tape despite 100-degree shade.  
The logger reports "soda water" kicks, no rotten eggs in sight.  
The company man approves the tape overtime, but fines the pusher a missing pin.  
The doghouse reeks of flat beer though the rig runs straight diesel.
rounds.chars: Derrickhand; Mud Logger
rounds.story: The well had kicked naturally occurring, high-pressure CO2 from the Jackson Dome trend, explaining the "soda water" gas readings and the carbonic acid turning the mud pits into a brewery. Because CO2 expands with intense Joule-Thomson cooling at surface temperatures—unlike methane which warms—the vent line froze solid in the 100-degree heat, blocking the separator and forcing the derrickhand to insulate it to prevent an overpressure explosion on the shale shakers.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Earl, the toolpusher

**Character 2:** Rosa, the derrickhand (occupation: derrickhand)

**Story:** The well has drilled into a pocket of carbon dioxide rather than sour gas, which explains the fizzy "soda water" kicks with no rotten-egg smell, and the rapidly expanding CO₂ chills the vent line until it freezes solid with dry ice even in 100-degree heat, so Rosa wraps it in heat tape and the company man gladly approves the overtime. Meanwhile, Earl has been home-brewing beer in the doghouse and pulled the pin from the rig's CO₂ fire extinguisher to carbonate it, but the batch went flat and stinks up the shack. The company man fined him for the missing safety pin.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Although the Jackson Dome does produce natural CO2 and CO2 expansion does cause Joule-Thomson cooling, the claim that methane warms on expansion at surface conditions is wrong (it cools too, just less), and the proposed fix of insulating a vent line to stop freezing is backwards, since insulation would worsen the cold and the "brewery" and "soda water" details are embellished beyond a coherent mechanism.

opus.judge:
B
Story B accounts for every clue, including the pusher's fine for the missing extinguisher pin and the flat-beer smell from his failed home brew, while Story A never explains the fine.

A

Story A accounts for every clue, including the company man's fine for the missing pin and the flat-beer smell in the doghouse, while Story B never explains the pin or the fine.

sol.judge:
B
It explains the fizzy kicks, lack of sulfur odor, and need for heat tape, while linking the missing extinguisher pin and flat-beer smell to the same brewing mishap.

A
Both stories link the fizzy kicks and freezing vent line to CO₂, but A also explains the approved overtime, the fine for the missing pin, and why the doghouse smells like flat beer.

rounds.riddle:
During a Kenyan marathon camp in Iten on 30 September 2017, Eliud Kipchoge finished in 2:00:25.
Seventeen pacemakers took turns, and a pushchair carried Kipchoge at the start.
Why could the performance not be ratified as a world record?
rounds.chars: Eliud Kipchoge; Patrick Sang (coach)
rounds.story: This was the INEOS 1:59 Challenge at Iten on 30 September 2017, when Eliud Kipchoge, coached by Patrick Sang, ran 2:00:25 with seventeen rotating pacemakers after being pushed in a pushchair at the start. The IAAF (now World Athletics) record rules permit only one official pacemaker to assist a record attempt and do not treat a pushchair as an approved pacing aid, so the seventeen pacemakers and pushchair made the run ineligible for ratification.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Baby Eliud Kipchoge, a toddler named after the famous runner.
**Character 2:** His father, Joseph, an athletics coach at the Iten training camp.

**Story:** At the camp's charity fun-day, Joseph strapped his little namesake son into a pushchair while seventeen of his athletes took turns pushing and pacing him around the course, crossing the line in 2:00:25. It could never be a world record because the "Eliud Kipchoge" in the result was a toddler who was pushed rather than running, in an unofficial, unsanctioned event, not the real champion.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The details are wrong: the 2:00:25 run was the Nike Breaking2 attempt at Monza on 6 May 2017 (not INEOS at Iten, and not 30 September), and the INEOS 1:59 Challenge in Vienna on 12 October 2019 was the sub-2 run (1:59:40). The ineligibility rationale is also wrong: record rules bar rotating or externally-aided pacing, not "only one pacemaker," and there was no pushchair.

opus.judge:
A

Story A naturally explains every odd detail: a toddler namesake in a pushchair, pushed by seventeen athletes at an unofficial camp event. Story B relies on false history (the INEOS 1:59 Challenge was in Vienna in 2019) and never explains why an elite runner would be in a pushchair.

B

Story B accounts for every odd detail, including the pushchair, the seventeen pacers, and the unofficial camp setting. Story A relies on invented rules and misplaces the INEOS challenge, which actually took place in Vienna in 2019.

sol.judge:
A
The toddler namesake explains the pushchair and the rotating pacemakers naturally: they pushed him around the course, so the finishing time was not a marathon running record.

B
The toddler namesake explains the pushchair and the seventeen helpers’ turns, while being pushed rather than running explains why his finish time could not count as a marathon record.

rounds.riddle:
Our silver fish run true when hunting in the North,
They wait beneath the merchant's heavy, iron spine.
But cross the hidden boundary to the bitter South,
The vanguard's eye sees heaven, and blows before the mark.
rounds.chars: Captain; Torpedoman
rounds.story: Realizing the Mark 6 magnetic explainer was calibrated for the Northern Hemisphere's downward vertical magnetic field and thus detonated prematurely in the Southern Hemisphere where the field points upward, the Captain identified the torpedo's upward-looking antenna as the culprit. He ordered the Torpedoman to physically sever the explainer's vertical antenna circuit, forcing the warheads to rely solely on the contact pistol so they would finally strike the merchant's iron spine instead of exploding before the mark.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kapitän Weber, a U-boat commander.
**Character 2:** Dr. Hartmann, a torpedo engineer who calibrated the magnetic exploders in Kiel.

**Story:** Hartmann's torpedoes, whose magnetic pistols were tuned to the downward-pointing magnetic field of northern waters, ran true and burst beneath the iron keels of merchant ships in the North Atlantic. But once Weber's boat crossed the magnetic equator into the South Atlantic, the field's dip reversed and pointed up toward the sky, so the sensor in each warhead's nose misread it and the torpedoes exploded prematurely, well short of their targets.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The Mark 6 magnetic exploder was real and had well-documented premature detonation and dud problems, and the Navy did deactivate it in 1943, but it sensed changes in the vertical component of the magnetic field with a coil, not an "upward-looking antenna" that could be severed, and the premature-firing fix was simply to disable the magnetic feature (by a procedure of deactivating it, e.g., changing settings or removing/ignoring it), not cutting an antenna circuit; the claim that it was calibrated for Northern Hemisphere and failed due to the Southern Hemisphere's upward field is a partial truth (latitude-dependent field was a real concern), but the specific mechanism as described is materially wrong.

opus.judge:
A
Story A covers every line of the riddle with no added plot: torpedoes run true in the North, burst beneath iron keels, and fire early once they cross the magnetic equator. Story B adds a fix that the riddle never mentions, garbles "exploder" as "explainer," and invents an antenna.

B
Story B maps every line directly (torpedoes working under keels in the North, crossing the magnetic equator, the nose sensor reading the reversed upward field and exploding early), while Story A adds an unrequested fix and an odd "upward-looking antenna."

sol.judge:
A
It explains the under-keel explosions, the hidden magnetic boundary, and the nose sensor’s premature triggering without inventing a repair that the riddle never mentions.

B
It ties the hidden boundary to the magnetic equator and the vanguard’s skyward gaze to the nose sensor’s misreading, explaining the premature blasts without adding an unmentioned repair.

rounds.riddle:
In our Tokyo sumo stable, Kenji scrubs the communal floor and eats last.
On Tuesday morning, Takeshi spends an extra hour shaping Kenji's hair into the grand ginkgo-leaf fan of the top ranks.
That afternoon, Kenji steps onto the clay for a single bout.
On Wednesday morning, Kenji scrubs the floor again, and Takeshi ties his hair back into a plain knot.
rounds.chars: Kenji; Takeshi (sumo hairdresser)
rounds.story: Kenji is a lower-ranked makushita wrestler in a Tokyo sumo stable, and Takeshi is the stable's hairdresser (tokoyama), who normally styles the grand oicho-mage topknot only for salaried top-division sekitori.
