When an injury in the second-highest division (Juryo) leaves an odd number of competitors on Tuesday, Japan Sumo Association rules tap top-ranked makushita Kenji to fill in for one Juryo bout—the single day he is permitted to wear the sekitori topknot before returning to his plain chonmage and chores on Wednesday.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kenji, a low-ranked makushita wrestler.
**Character 2:** Takeshi, the stable's tokoyama (sumo hairdresser).

**Story:** On Tuesday Kenji was called up to fill a gap on the jūryō schedule, and sumo rules require a lower-ranked wrestler fighting a salaried sekitori to wear the ōichō-mage ginkgo topknot, so Takeshi styled it for that one bout. With the bout done, Kenji went back to being an ordinary apprentice on Wednesday, scrubbing floors and wearing his plain chonmage again.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Sumo does have this mechanism: when a Juryo wrestler is injured and the day's bouts come out uneven, the JSA can call up a top-ranked makushita wrestler to fill in, and tokoyama do style the oicho-mage for sekitori while lower ranks wear a plain chonmage. The details are embellished, but the core process is real. Wrestlers in the makushita division can wear the oicho-mage for special occasions, such as when fighting a Juryo wrestler, and a makushita wrestler called up this way does fight in a Juryo bout.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle is set in a Tokyo sumo stable, with wrestlers scrubbing the communal floor, eating last, bouting on the clay, and a stable hairdresser styling topknots.

opus.judge:
A

Story A explains why Kenji was called up (an injury left an odd number of jūryō wrestlers) and correctly makes him a top-ranked makushita, whereas Story B calls him "low-ranked" and gives no cause for the vacancy.

B
Story B explains more of the riddle: an injury leaves an odd number of Jūryō wrestlers, so a top makushita fills in for one bout, which accounts for the single bout and the one-day topknot. Story A just asserts a "gap" without saying why it arose.

sol.judge:
A
The injury explains why Kenji was called up for exactly one jūryō bout, and the temporary exception explains his elaborate topknot without changing his rank or chores.

A
It ties the formal topknot to the specific bout rather than a day-long exception, explaining why Kenji returns to his plain knot and chores without any change in rank.

rounds.riddle:
On a Texas oil rig, Cal dropped a pinch of grit into the drillpipe at stroke zero.
At stroke 1,200, a gas spike flashed on Jo’s screen.
At stroke 1,500, a fossil chip came over the shaker; Jo penciled in 600, not 300.
She didn’t correct for the hour the pumps sat idle at lunch.
rounds.chars: Cal; Jo (mud logger)
rounds.story: Cal’s grit was calcium carbide, a tracer that releases acetylene on contact with water, and Jo used its return to estimate when the bit had cut the fossil chip. The tracer’s 1,200-stroke trip included 300 strokes down the drillpipe, but the chip started at the bit and only had to come back up, so Jo subtracted 900 from 1,500 and ignored lunch because idle pumps add no strokes.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Cal, a roughneck on the drill floor.

**Character 2:** Jo, a mud logger.

**Story:** Cal dropped calcium carbide "grit" into the drillpipe as a lag test. It fizzed into acetylene gas when it hit the mud, and when the spike showed up at stroke 1,200 Jo subtracted the known 300 strokes it takes to pump down the pipe, giving 900 strokes for cuttings to ride up from the bit. So when the fossil chip crossed the shaker at stroke 1,500, she logged it as rock cut at stroke 600 (1,500 − 900), not 300, and she ignored the idle lunch hour because cuttings only move when the pumps stroke, so lag is counted in strokes, not clock time.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Calcium carbide is a documented tracer in mud logging: it reacts with water to release acetylene, which is detected at the surface to measure lag time. Counting pump strokes to compute lag, by subtracting the downward trip through the drillpipe and counting only the annulus return, is standard practice, and idle pumps add no strokes.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle opens by explicitly setting the scene on a Texas oil rig, and its characters, drillpipe, shaker, pumps, and mud logging all belong to that setting.

opus.judge:
B

Story B explicitly works through how the 1,200-stroke total minus the known 300 down-pipe strokes gives a 900-stroke lag, how 1,500 − 900 yields 600 (not the naive 300), and why the idle lunch hour doesn't matter, while Story A reaches the same answer less clearly.

A

Story A spells out the full chain: carbide producing acetylene, subtracting the 300 pipe strokes to get a 900-stroke annular lag, the 1,500 − 900 = 600 result, and why idle lunch time doesn't matter. Story B makes the same points more tersely.

sol.judge:
B
It explicitly explains why Jo logged 600 rather than 300: the tracer’s 1,200 strokes included 300 down the pipe, while the chip took only the 900-stroke return trip, and lunch added no strokes.

A
It explains the gas spike as the carbide tracer’s return and explicitly shows why Jo subtracted only the 900-stroke return lag, getting 600 rather than 300, with no strokes added during lunch.

rounds.riddle:
At our marathon camp in Iten, Kenya, I handed the same woman two warm cups an hour apart.
She read 1.004 both times; the second cup held just one millilitre more than the first.
She sealed what I’d given her both times. Why did she make me stay after 149 millilitres but not after 150?
rounds.chars: Kiptoo; Wanjiku (doping control officer)
rounds.story: Wanjiku was collecting urine for a doping test, so she sealed Kiptoo’s first sample but kept him there to provide another because the first was too dilute. Under anti-doping rules, the minimum specific gravity measured by refractometer drops from 1.005 to 1.003 when a single sample reaches 150 millilitres, so the extra millilitre let him leave without his urine getting any more concentrated.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Me, a marathon runner training at the Iten camp.
**Character 2:** The woman, a doping control officer conducting surprise out-of-competition urine tests.

**Story:** Both of my warm urine samples read 1.004 on her refractometer, below the specific-gravity threshold for a properly concentrated sample. She sealed each one anyway, but the 149 mL sample fell under the volume line she treated as enough for the lab to work with a dilute sample, so I had to stay and keep giving more. The 150 mL sample met that line, so she sealed it and let me go back to training.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

WADA's rules require a suitable specific gravity of at least 1.005 by refractometer (or 1.010 by lab), and a sample volume of at least 90 mL. There is no provision lowering the threshold to 1.003 once a sample reaches 150 mL, so the described mechanism is fabricated.

rounds.story: The overseas buyer adds a teaspoon of another distillery's whisky to his cask—an industry practice called "teaspooning"—to legally reclassify it from a Single Malt to a Blended Malt. **Character 2:** Hamish, the distillery manager

"Teaspooning" is a real practice, but it is used to stop a malt being sold as "single malt" (for example, to avoid brand association), and the 2009 regulations do not ban exporting Scotch in casks. They require Single Malt Scotch Whisky to be bottled in Scotland, but blended malt can be exported in bulk, and the claim that no Scotch may be exported in wooden casks is wrong. So the mechanism is partly based on real rules but is materially wrong as described.

**Character 1:** Seaman Joe Kowalski, holding four fives (twenty pips, five to a card) and needing just one point to win.

**Character 2:** Torpedoman's Mate Eddie Reyes, the dealer, needing two points.

**Story:** Playing cribbage on a homemade board for the crew's last tin of peaches, Joe sat on four fives, a hand worth at least 20 and possibly 29, and needed only one peg to win. rounds.fact:

The cribbage rule is real (the dealer scores 2 points "for his heels" when a jack is turned as the starter), but the scenario has a fatal flaw: Eddie couldn't have "cut" the jack and also held all four fives plus that jack, since the starter would be a different card from his hand's jack, and a 28-point hand requires three fives plus the jack of the starter's suit... actually, a 28 hand is three fives plus a jack of the same suit as the starter five, with the starter being the fifth card, so it's four fives with a jack starter being 29 at best, not matching the described hand. Specifically, four fives plus a jack starter is a 29 hand, not 28, and the jack-starter "nobs" doesn't apply. Also, "Lou pegged out" from 2 points implies he was already at 119 or so, which is not stated, so the mechanism is materially wrong in its details.

Out of Ísafjörður, Jón watches their nets spill tonnes of unquoted haddock onto the deck, yet Magnús forbids him to shovel a single fish back into the sea.
A gale is rising and Jón begs to steam for port, but Magnús orders the trawl dropped again and again through the freezing spray.

rounds.chars: Jón; Magnús (trawler skipper)
rounds.story: Because Iceland strictly prohibits discarding fish at sea, Magnús cannot dump the unquoted haddock overboard and must land every kilo at port. Under Iceland's VS-afli (VS-catch) rule, a trawler may land unquoted bycatch without quota penalties—receiving 20% of the auction price while 80% goes to a marine research fund—only if it stays at or below 5% of the trip's total weight, so Magnús braves the gale to catch nineteen times that haul in legal fish before heading home.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Jón, a young deckhand.
**Character 2:** Magnús, a trawler skipper who knows Iceland's fisheries law.

**Story:** Iceland bans throwing fish back, so Magnús must land the unquoted haddock. The law lets a boat land such "VS-catch" only if it is at most 5% of the trip's total, with the boat keeping 20% of its value and the rest going to a state fund. So he braved the gale until the total catch passed twenty times the haddock's weight, which made the haddock legal instead of a heavy fine, and he happily took his fifth at the dock.
rounds.fact:
REAL: Iceland does have a discard ban and a VS-afli (Verðmætasjóður/"value-based" catch) rule under which landed catch not covered by quota is sold at auction, with the vessel keeping about 20% of the proceeds and the rest going to a marine research fund (Verkefnasjóður sjávarútvegsins).

The main inaccuracy is the cap: the VS-afli allowance is not exactly 5% of the trip's total weight (it is generally tied to a percentage of catch, around 5% of the total catch by species, with some variation), but the overall mechanism is correct enough.

rounds.riddle:
In Paris, Henri vows to leave the ovens cold at dawn unless his pay is raised, certain he cannot be fired.
That evening, Claire puts a neighbor on the payroll, yet keeps the shutters locked all morning while paying him to read at the empty counter.
No union has called a national strike, and not a pinch of flour is touched.
By dusk, Henri is legally dismissed.
rounds.chars: Claire; Henri (baker)
rounds.story: Henri had been the sole employee at Claire's Paris bakery, where French labor law uniquely allows a lone worker to strike alone, whereas in any workplace with two or more employees a solo walkout without a national union strike call is an illegal absence. By putting a neighbor on the payroll the night before—without needing to open the shop or have him replace Henri at the ovens—Claire stripped Henri of his sole-employee status so she could legally fire him the moment he refused to work.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Henri, the lone baker at a small Paris bakery.

**Character 2:** Claire, the bakery's owner (an employer who knows French labor law).

**Story:** Henri was sure his dawn walkout was a protected strike, because French law lets a sole employee strike, but only when joining a national strike call. That evening Claire hired a neighbor, so the shop now had two workers; at dawn the neighbor stayed at the empty counter and kept working by reading, which made Henri's stoppage a one-man refusal rather than a collective strike, and with no national strike to join, Claire lawfully fired him for unjustified absence by dusk.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

French law does protect the right to strike, and a single-employee company can lawfully strike, but it does not work as described: in the private sector a strike needs a collective work stoppage with professional demands, and hiring a neighbor would not strip the right to strike or make firing a striker lawful (dismissing someone for striking is void, barring serious misconduct "faute lourde").
rounds.fit_reason:

The riddle is clearly about a Paris bakery strike: Henri threatens to stop work at the ovens unless his pay rises, and the plot centers on the strike and his dismissal at a Paris bakery.

opus.judge:

Story B gives a coherent legal mechanism: hiring the neighbor ends Henri's lone-employee right to strike alone, and with no national strike call his walkout becomes an unjustified absence. Story A's version of the law is self-contradictory, since it says a sole employee may strike only by joining a national call, which makes hiring the neighbor pointless.

Story A explains why hiring the neighbor matters: it ends Henri's sole-employee protection, so the shop never needs to open and he can be fired. Story B contradicts itself, because if a lone employee could strike only by joining a national call, Henri was unprotected before the hire and the neighbor would be pointless.

sol.judge:
B
It correctly treats sole-employee status as an exception to the collective-strike requirement and explains why Claire needed the neighbor on payroll but not at the ovens.

A

A explains why hiring the neighbor mattered even though he never touched the flour, whereas B makes the hire unnecessary by requiring a national strike call even for a sole employee.

rounds.riddle:
In the North Atlantic in 1943, two men aboard a submerged U-boat watched the same needle fall.
One said, “We’re sinking”; the other said, “No, we’re leaking.”
With the depth gauge steady and the sea shut out, the second man went looking for air coming in.
rounds.chars: Emil; Otto (submarine engineer)
rounds.story: Emil had mistaken the control-room barometer for a depth gauge, but Otto was watching it because the crew had raised the air pressure inside the boat slightly to check its seals. The barometer measured cabin pressure, not water pressure, so its falling needle betrayed air escaping from the pressurized compartment, and Otto checked the next compartment for air leaking into it.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** A young seaman (Matrosengefreiter) on his first patrol.

**Character 2:** The Leitender Ingenieur, the U-boat's chief engineer.

**Story:** The falling needle was not the depth gauge but the pressure gauge on the boat's high-pressure air flasks. The seaman thought losing blow-air meant they could never surface, but the chief, seeing the depth gauge steady and the hull dry, knew the air was escaping from a cracked fitting into the boat itself, so he went listening for the hiss of air coming in.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Submarines can be slightly pressurized to test hull and compartment seals, and a falling air-pressure reading on a barometer (or manometer) indicates leakage, so the described mechanism works roughly as stated.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle is set in 1943 aboard a submerged U-boat, a submarine with a crew, which matches the request. It also centers on two crew members and their shared problem, so it is clearly about a submarine crew in that year.

opus.judge:

Story B fits most naturally: a falling HP-air flask gauge reads as "we can't surface," the steady depth gauge and dry hull rule out sinking, and air escaping into the boat is exactly the "air coming in" he goes looking for.

A

Story A fits best: the falling needle is the air-flask gauge, so with a steady depth gauge and a dry hull, the escaping air must be hissing into the boat. Story B is weaker because a falling cabin-pressure needle mistaken for a depth gauge would suggest rising, not sinking.

sol.judge:
B
The falling flask pressure explains both the seaman’s fear that they couldn’t surface and the engineer’s search for air leaking into the boat, even though its depth was steady and no seawater was entering.

A
A falling air-flask pressure explains the leak and why the engineer looked for air entering the dry hull, while the seaman’s fear of losing the ability to surface explains his alarm despite the steady depth gauge.

rounds.riddle:
Deep under a 1943 depth-charge run, a fierce hiss filled the sealed control room as the depth needle climbed thirty feet shallower.
Though the deck stayed dead level, Cole reached for the flood valve to drive the submarine back down.
Swallowing hard to clear his ears, Miller slapped Cole's hand away and spun a brass wheel overhead.
"Keep her level," Miller barked. "We haven't risen an inch."
rounds.chars: Cole; Miller (chief machinist's mate)
rounds.story: The depth-charge concussion ruptured a high-pressure air line in the sealed control room, raising the cabin air pressure by nearly one atmosphere and popping Miller's ears before he shut the overhead isolation valve. Because WWII submarine Bourdon-tube depth gauges measure the difference between outside seawater pressure and inside cabin air pressure, that excess cabin pressure fooled the needle into reading thirty feet shallower, so Miller stopped Cole from flooding the trim tank and driving their level boat deeper toward crush depth.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Cole, a young planesman on his first war patrol.
**Character 2:** Miller, the submarine's veteran Chief of the Boat.

**Story:** A depth charge cracked a high-pressure air line, so air hissed into the sealed control room and raised its pressure. The depth gauge measures sea pressure against cabin pressure, so it falsely showed the boat rising. Miller felt that rise in his ears and saw the deck stay level, so he knew they hadn't moved; he stopped Cole from flooding the boat toward crush depth and spun the overhead valve shut to stop the leak.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
WWII submarine depth gauges did read the difference between sea pressure and internal pressure, so raised cabin pressure would make them read shallower, but a ~1 atm rise would shift the reading by about 33 feet, so that part is roughly right. The problem is that a depth-charge-ruptured high-pressure air line raising pressure by nearly a full atmosphere in a control room is implausible, and the described sequence is not an established mechanism. Also, the actual depth gauges were typically referenced to the boat's internal pressure only loosely, and the scenario's details are embellished beyond what the real mechanism supports.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES

The riddle is clearly set in 1943, with the opening line naming a "1943 depth-charge run." It is also clearly about a submarine crew, with a sealed control room, a depth needle, a flood valve, a trim tank, and two named crewmen, Cole and Miller.

opus.judge:
A
Story A ties every detail together most precisely: about one atmosphere of extra cabin pressure, roughly 33 feet of seawater, explains the exact thirty-foot false reading, while the ruptured air line covers the hiss, Miller's ears and the overhead isolation valve.

B

Story B explains the exact thirty-foot error, since nearly one atmosphere of extra cabin pressure equals about 33 feet of seawater on a differential Bourdon-tube gauge, and it accounts for the hiss, ears, overhead valve and level boat as fully as Story A does.

sol.judge:
A
It ties the thirty-foot false reading to a nearly one-atmosphere rise in cabin pressure and identifies the brass wheel as the air-line shutoff, without treating a level deck as proof that the submarine hadn’t risen.

B
It ties the thirty-foot false reading to a cabin pressure rise of nearly one atmosphere, explaining the hiss, Miller’s ear pressure, and why he shut the overhead valve instead of letting Cole flood the trim tank.

rounds.chars: A submarine sailor; his commander (U-boat captain)
rounds.story: While submerged in 1943, the crew had to load a dead sailor and heavy iron ballast into a torpedo tube—reclaiming his bunk from food storage—just to conduct a secret burial without leaving floating debris that would betray their position. Because standard German G7e torpedoes were launched by an internal tail-piston that struck a 22-inch-long rear guide-trough, the captain ordered the corpse's lower legs sawed off so the steel ram could seat behind the body without crushing it and jamming the firing valve.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The narrator, a WWII submarine crewman.
**Character 2:** Petty Officer Harris, the boat's cook, a short man with iron leg braces, who died on patrol.

**Story:** In 1943, when Harris died at sea, we couldn't fire him from the torpedo tube without giving away our position, so I unbolted his iron braces (sawing through his frozen trouser shins) to fit him into the cold-storage locker, and I stacked the displaced food in his empty bunk to keep the boat's trim balanced. He rode home that way and was carried ashore at port, leaving no burial wake and never touching the sea.
rounds.fact:

Burials at sea from U-boats did sometimes use torpedo tubes, but the G7e was an electric torpedo launched by compressed air (not an internal tail-piston striking a guide-trough), and the claim of sawing off a corpse's legs to seat a "steel ram" is fabricated.

The riddle explicitly places itself in 1943 with "Beneath the waves of forty-three," and its imagery (a boat, a torpedo tube, bunks, a crew leaving "without a wake" and never touching "the sea outside") clearly describes a submarine crew.

Story A keeps the body aboard, which explains "never touched the sea outside" and "without a wake," while Story B fires the corpse out of the tube, contradicting that line and relying on a contrived piston explanation for the sawing.

B
Story B fits every line naturally: the iron braces explain the "iron fate," the food moved into his bunk keeps the trim balanced, the sawing removes the braces (not needed for size, since "the tube was wide"), and keeping him aboard explains "never touched the sea"; Story A contradicts that last line by firing him out of the tube and relies on invented torpedo mechanics.

sol.judge:

The braces and cold-storage locker explain the sawing despite the wide tube, the displaced food goes into the bunk, and carrying him ashore accounts for both the lack of a wake and his never touching the sea.

B
Storing the body in the food locker explains why the food went into his bunk and why he was carried ashore without ever touching seawater, while the iron braces give a reason for the sawing despite his short stature.

rounds.riddle:
Off east Iceland, the main screen blazes red to port, while starboard shows only a pale gray mist.
Einar points port, but the older man checks a second display where the mist glows brighter, and steers straight into it.
"Land that red cloud in Neskaupstaður and we're ruined," he mutters, lowering the net.
An hour later, the trawler's hold is brimming with silver.
rounds.chars: Einar; the older man (skipper)
rounds.story: The trawler has exhausted its herring quota, so under Iceland's strict quota and no-discard laws, catching the dense herring shoal to port would bring ruinous penalties at Neskaupstaður. Because Atlantic mackerel lack the air-filled swim bladders that make herring blaze red on standard low-frequency (38 kHz) sonar, the skipper confirms the faint starboard mist is a massive mackerel school on the high-frequency (200 kHz) display—where bladderless mackerel reflect far more strongly—and hauls in a legal catch.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Einar, a young deckhand on his first season.

**Character 2:** Gunnar, the veteran skipper of the trawler (occupation: fishing captain).

**Story:** The main sonar showed a huge red school to port, but Gunnar's second echo-sounder, set to a different frequency, revealed it as mackerel, a species whose quota they had already used up, so landing it at the Neskaupstaður processing plant would bring ruinous fines and confiscation. The faint gray "mist" to starboard glowed bright on that second screen, which marked it as a dense herring school, so he shot the net there and filled the hold with silver herring.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Mackerel lack swim bladders, so they reflect weakly at 38 kHz, but that doesn't make them reflect more strongly at 200 kHz; bladderless fish are weak targets at all frequencies, and the claim that herring "blaze red" because of their swim bladders while mackerel show up better at high frequency is backwards or materially wrong, even though Iceland's quota and discard rules are real.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle is set on an Icelandic fishing trawler off east Iceland, near Neskaupstaður, and centers on the fishing activity the user requested.

opus.judge:
A

Story A's acoustics are correct: swim-bladdered herring glow red at 38 kHz while bladderless mackerel appear faint there but brighter at 200 kHz. Story B reverses this, having the mackerel blaze red and the herring look faint, which contradicts the physics the riddle depends on.

B

Story B gives a real acoustic reason why the shoal blazes red on the main screen but shows as faint mist that glows brighter on the second display: swim-bladdered herring echo strongly at 38 kHz, while bladderless mackerel echo more strongly at 200 kHz. Story A asserts the frequency difference without that physical logic, and its version is backwards, since herring would echo strongly rather than faintly.

sol.judge:
A
Herring’s swim bladders explain the strong red return on the main sonar, while the higher-frequency display reveals the legal mackerel catch that Einar nearly overlooks.

B
The contrast between herring’s strong low-frequency echo and mackerel’s weaker one explains the two displays, while the exhausted herring quota explains why the skipper passes up the red school for a legal catch of silvery mackerel.

rounds.riddle:
At a Kochi wedding hall, a guest weighs the groom's heavy *kasumala*, dips it in a brimming bowl, and nods at the spill.
Then he holds a tiny silver cylinder beside the hanging gold coins and watches one subtly lean toward his hand.
Before the *thali* can be tied next to the *nilavilakku*, he pockets the necklace and halts the ceremony.
"It passed the water," he tells the stunned crowd, "but real gold never leans."
rounds.chars: the groom; the bride's uncle (goldsmith)
rounds.story: Hoping to pass off cheap counterfeits at his Kochi wedding, the groom gifted a *kasumala* made of gold-plated tungsten, whose density (19.25 g/cm³) closely matches pure gold (19.3 g/cm³) and fooled the scale and water-displacement test. However, the bride's uncle, a goldsmith, knew that while gold is diamagnetic and weakly repelled by a magnetic field, tungsten is paramagnetic—so when he held a strong neodymium magnet near the hanging coins and saw one lean toward it, he exposed the fraud and halted the ceremony.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Ravi, the groom's uncle, who supplied the "heirloom" kasumala.

**Character 2:** Thomas, a gold assayer at a Kochi bank and the bride's cousin.

**Story:** Ravi had secretly pawned the family's real kasumala and replaced it with a forgery: dense tungsten cores, which displace water like true gold, plated in gold, but with a few coins padded out with cheap nickel-steel. Thomas's displacement test came out right, yet when his tiny neodymium magnet made one coin lean, he knew that non-magnetic gold would never move and halted the wedding before the bride's family could be cheated.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Tungsten's density (19.25 g/cm³) really does nearly match gold's (19.3 g/cm³), so gold-plated tungsten is a known counterfeiting method. Gold is diamagnetic and tungsten is weakly paramagnetic, so a strong magnet can distinguish them, though the effect is very small and a coin "leaning" toward a magnet would be a dramatic embellishment.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES

The riddle is set at a "Kochi wedding hall" and uses Kerala-specific wedding elements: the *kasumala* (a gold necklace), the *thali* (the tied wedding pendant), and the *nilavilakku* (a traditional lamp). Together these clearly place it at a Kerala wedding.

opus.judge:
A
Story A's nickel-steel padding in a few coins explains why only one coin leaned toward the magnet, while Story B relies on tungsten's paramagnetism, which is far too weak to make a coin visibly lean.

B
Story B explains why only one coin leaned (it was padded with ferromagnetic nickel-steel), whereas Story A relies on tungsten's paramagnetism, which is far too weak to make a coin visibly lean and would affect every coin, not just one.

sol.judge:
A
The tungsten cores explain why the necklace passed the density test, while a nickel-steel insert explains why the tiny magnet visibly pulled one coin toward it far better than tungsten’s weak paramagnetism does.

B
The near-gold density explains why the necklace passed the water test, while a nickel-steel insert explains why one coin visibly leaned toward the tiny magnet.

rounds.riddle:
Five weeks out of Reykjavík, north of Vestmannaeyjar, our trawler's hold reeks of ammonia and clanks with steel plates.
At dawn the pick of the trip was split: gutted whole cod went straight into those plates, but fillets cut from the very same fish were banned from them.
Grimsby cabled double money for "the freshest"; the man in yellow oilskins cabled back, "You'll have Tuesday's, never today's."
Today's fillets lay in slush ice a full twenty-four hours before freezing, while older, duller flesh went in first — why?
rounds.chars: Hrefna, a Grimsby fish importer; Óli, the trawler's refrigeration engineer
rounds.story: Óli runs the ammonia plate-freezer plant on a factory trawler that lands nothing fresh, only frozen blocks five weeks later, so what Hrefna is really buying is how a block behaves in her thawing room, not hours out of the sea. Gutted cod can be frozen stiff pre-rigor because the backbone restrains the flesh, but a fillet freed from the spine and frozen before rigor has passed goes into thaw rigor on defrosting — contracting by up to a third of its length, turning tough and weeping red drip — so today's fillets must sit in 0 °C slush ice for the roughly twenty-four hours cod needs to come out of rigor, while yesterday's, already through it, freeze first.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Grímur, a Grimsby fish merchant who wants the freshest catch.

**Character 2:** Captain Einar, the trawler's skipper (the man in yellow oilskins), trained in fish technology.

**Story:** Einar knows that a cod filleted and plate-frozen before rigor mortis sets in will suffer "thaw rigor" when it defrosts: the loose muscle, freed from the skeleton, contracts violently, so the fillet shrinks, gapes, toughens and weeps its juice. Whole gutted fish can go straight into the ammonia plate freezers because the backbone holds the muscle in place. So he lets today's fillets pass through rigor in slush ice for a day first, and he cables Grimsby that the only top-quality fillets he can deliver are Tuesday's, not today's.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Thaw rigor is a documented phenomenon: fish fillets frozen before rigor mortis has passed contract strongly on thawing (reported up to about 30–50%), becoming tough and losing drip, so processors hold fillets until they are past rigor (or freeze whole gutted fish, where the backbone restrains the flesh).
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle is set on a trawler that leaves Reykjavík and sails past Vestmannaeyjar, both Icelandic places, and its whole plot concerns the vessel's catch, hold, and freezing processes.

opus.judge:
B

Both stories use the same thaw-rigor mechanism, but B also explains why "freshest" means nothing on a five-week factory trip that lands only frozen blocks, and it explicitly accounts for the older, already-through-rigor flesh going into the freezer first.

A

Both stories rely on thaw rigor, but A more fully explains why "freshest" is meaningless for a factory trawler landing frozen blocks five weeks later, and why yesterday's older fillets freeze first.

sol.judge:
A
Both stories explain the freezing order through thaw rigor, but A also explains the cable’s “Tuesday’s, never today’s”: the best fillets for Grimsby are the ones that have already passed through rigor, not the ones just caught.

A
Both explain thaw rigor, but A also explains why Grimsby’s premium for “the freshest” favors yesterday’s fillets: on a frozen-only trip, quality after thawing matters more than time since catch.

rounds.riddle:
In a Speyside bonded warehouse every young cask counts up to its third birthday, but the oldest one, says the woman with the keys, counts down.
Forty-six winters it has grown lighter, and nobody has ever topped it up, though it is barely a third full.
Her hydrometer reads 40.4, so she has booked the bottling hall for Tuesday — four days before that cask's forty-seventh birthday.
The collector offers double if she waits five years; the fierce three-year-old next door could lend it a cupful, and she forbids it.
rounds.chars: Fergus, a collector from Geneva; Morag, the distillery's bonded-warehouse keeper
rounds.story: Morag's dunnage warehouse is cold and damp, so the angel's share steals ethanol faster than water — the reverse of a hot, dry Kentucky rickhouse, where strength climbs — and this cask, filled at the standard 63.5%, has shed about half a point of ABV every year for forty-six years down to 40.4%. The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 both bar anything under 40% ABV from being called Scotch whisky and force an age statement to name the youngest spirit in the bottle, so she must bottle before the cask's forty-seventh birthday, when it legally becomes a near-worthless "spirit drink": Fergus's five extra years would destroy it, a topping-up of water only hastens the fall, and a cup of the fierce three-year-old would rescue the strength solely by relabelling forty-six years old as three.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Morag, the warehouse manager and cellar master who holds the keys.
**Character 2:** Mr. Hale, a wealthy whisky collector.

**Story:** Young spirit counts *up* to three years, when it may legally be called Scotch whisky. Morag's 46-year-old cask counts *down*, because its alcohol has evaporated over decades to 40.4%, and once it slips below 40% it can never legally be Scotch whisky again. So she bottles it on Tuesday, while it is still a 46-year-old Scotch, and refuses Hale's double offer to wait five years, which would leave it too weak to be whisky at all. She also forbids "topping it up" with the strong three-year-old next door, because a single cupful would make the whole cask's legal age statement just three years.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Scotch whisky must be at least 40% ABV under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, and age statements must refer to the youngest spirit in the blend. Cool, damp Scottish warehouses do tend to lose alcohol faster than water, so ABV declines over decades, and casks filled around 63.5% are standard. The only quibble is the exact rate of loss, which is a minor detail.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle is set in a Speyside bonded warehouse and centers on a Scotch whisky cask, its aging, the distillery's keeper, and Scotch Whisky Regulations, so it is clearly about a Scottish whisky distillery.

opus.judge:
B

Story B explains every detail: the half-point-per-year loss in a damp dunnage warehouse accounts for the 40.4% reading and why the deadline falls at the forty-seventh birthday, and the 40% minimum and youngest-spirit age rules explain refusing both the collector's wait and the three-year-old's cupful, whereas Story A never explains why the bottling must happen just before that birthday.

A
Story A explains more of the odd details: why the strength falls (cold, damp dunnage), the steady yearly rate that brings it just under 40% around the forty-seventh birthday, and why topping up with water or young spirit won't work, whereas Story B leaves the birthday timing unexplained.

sol.judge:
A
It explains the three-year minimum, the countdown toward 40% ABV, and why adding younger whisky would sacrifice the age statement, without making the forty-seventh birthday a legal cutoff.

B
It explains the countdown to the 40% ABV threshold and why adding younger whisky would cost the cask its age statement, without treating the forty-seventh birthday itself as a legal cutoff.

rounds.riddle:
No fire, no priest — a government counter in Ernakulam, where we both rent rooms, pinned our names on a board for thirty days.
We filed there and not in Kottayam, where she was born, so that nobody at home would hear of it.
On the twenty-ninth day her father walked up from Kottayam with a photocopy of that same notice, which he said he had read at home, and demanded that it be stopped.
They told him he had no ground; then, since the counter wanted three witnesses and we had brought only two, he signed — and the photographer went back to his camera.
rounds.chars: Unni, the groom, a Nair draftsman renting in Ernakulam; the bride's father, a retired Village Officer from Kottayam
rounds.story: She is Syrian Christian and I am Nair, so we married under the Special Marriage Act and gave the thirty-day notice in Ernakulam, where we had both rented rooms for a year, sure that filing four districts from home would keep it secret. What we did not know is Section 6(3): the Marriage Officer must transmit a copy of every notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where a party permanently resides, who affixes it on his own board — so our names and her house address went up in Kottayam, where her father, thirty years in the revenue office, recognised the procedure, read it, and came on the twenty-ninth day, inside the objection window; told that Section 7 permits objections only on age, bigamy, prohibited degrees or consent and never caste or religion, he instead supplied the third witness Section 12 requires, because we had brought only my cousin and the photographer.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Meera, the bride, born in Kottayam and renting a room in Ernakulam.
**Character 2:** Joseph, a wedding photographer hired by the couple, who had been about to step in as their missing third witness.

**Story:** Under the Special Marriage Act, the Ernakulam marriage officer had to send a copy of the couple's 30-day notice to the registrar in Kottayam, where Meera permanently resided, and it was posted there too, so her father read it on the public board and came on the last day to object. The officer told him an objection must rest on a legal bar such as age, an existing spouse or prohibited kinship, and he had none; so, beaten and softening, he took the pen and signed as the required third witness himself, freeing Joseph to go back to photographing the wedding.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Under the Special Marriage Act 1954, Section 5 notice goes to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one party has resided for 30 days, and Section 6(2) requires him to publish it on his board, but Section 6(3) says that if either party is not permanently residing in that officer's district, a copy must be transmitted to the Marriage Officer of the district of permanent residence for affixing. So the transmission is real. The inaccuracies are elsewhere: Section 7 objections are not limited to age, bigamy, prohibited degrees, and consent. Section 4 conditions include monogamy, soundness of mind, age, and prohibited degrees, so the list is roughly right. But the core of the story is the third witness, and Section 12 requires three witnesses at solemnization, which is real. Kerala also has rules, and the claimed "Village Officer" background is flavor. The mechanism is therefore roughly correct, though my first line was wrong.

REAL

The Section 6(3) transmission to the district of permanent residence, the Section 7 limits on objections, and the three witnesses required under Section 12 all work roughly as described.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES
The riddle is set in Kerala, since Ernakulam and Kottayam are both Kerala districts, and it is about a wedding. "No fire, no priest," the thirty-day notice, the witnesses, and the photographer all point to a civil marriage ceremony, though the wedding is implied rather than named outright.

opus.judge:
A
Story A explains why "the photographer went back to his camera": the father took the photographer's place as the third witness. In Story B, the photographer was already one of the two witnesses, so the father signing would not free him, and B also wrongly places Ernakulam "four districts" from Kottayam.

A
Story A explains every detail more completely: the interfaith marriage accounts for "no fire, no priest" and the need for secrecy, Section 6(3) explains the Kottayam posting, the father's revenue-office background explains how he knew to read it, and the photographer as one of only two witnesses explains why a third was needed.

sol.judge:
A
It explains both how the notice reached Kottayam and why the photographer went back to his camera: the father took his place as the third witness.

B
Both stories explain how the notice reached Kottayam, but B better explains why the photographer went back to his camera: the father took the witness slot the photographer was about to fill.

rounds.riddle:
We paid for thirty-one nights in a Wayanad hill town where nobody had heard of either family, and we told not one relative.
No priest, no thali, no fire — two signatures, three witnesses fetched off the tea-shop bench, and the man at the desk pinning our names to his wall.
On the eleventh morning her father drove in from three hundred kilometres away and recited that notice back to us, word for word, though we had sent him nothing.

It accounts for the three earlier duds on the same patrol and ties them directly to the captain’s decision to sacrifice the textbook angle and recommend the same workaround fleetwide.

rounds.riddle:
September 1943, north of New Britain: Duda's textbook fish struck the freighter dead square on the beam at 900 yards — we heard the clang, and she kept steaming.
His botched one, raking her flank at a shallow slant, tore her open, and we cheered the worst-aimed shot of the patrol.
Pike's report formally requested permission to attack at worse angles, and in November Pearl sent our cure: a replacement part one third the weight of the piece it replaced.
Who are we, and why did the perfect shot fail while the botch killed?
rounds.chars: Hollis Pike (submarine skipper); Ray "Clang" Duda
rounds.story: Pike's boat was shooting the scandalous Mark 14 torpedo, and since Nimitz had deactivated its premature-firing magnetic feature in June 1943 only the Mark 6 contact pistol remained — which Duda's clanging square hit and killing glancing hit proved was itself defective. The little-known defect was inertia: the Mark 6's steel firing pin was so heavy that a perfect 90° impact decelerated the warhead violently enough to buckle the pin's guide rails and jam it, while a slanting hit slowed gently and fired normally — hence Pike's request for oblique attacks until Swede Momsen's Pearl Harbor shop issued aluminium firing pins machined from a shot-down Japanese plane's propeller, a third the mass and therefore too light to jam themselves.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Duda, torpedoman's mate aboard a U.S. fleet submarine.
**Character 2:** Lieutenant Commander Pike (occupation: submarine captain, who wrote the patrol report).

**Story:** Duda's perfect 90° hit failed because the Mark 6 exploder's heavy steel firing pin, slammed by the full head-on deceleration, bent and jammed in its guide before it could reach the detonator cap, while his glancing hit decelerated the torpedo more gently, so the pin slid free and fired. Pike's sarcastic request to shoot at "worse angles" joined a flood of similar complaints, and Pearl Harbor's tests confirmed the flaw, so the base machined a lightweight firing pin (reportedly from aluminum salvaged from downed Japanese aircraft propellers) roughly a third the weight of the old one, and the fleet's torpedoes finally exploded on square hits.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Mark 14 torpedo's contact exploder really did have a firing-pin problem (the Mark 6 pistol's pin jammed on near-perpendicular hits, and Nimitz did deactivate the magnetic feature in June 1943), but the fixes were a lighter firing pin or a modified pin mechanism, not aluminium pins from a Japanese propeller made in a "Momsen shop." The named characters and the aluminium-from-a-plane's-propeller detail are fabricated, so the story is materially wrong even though the underlying inertia defect is partly real.
rounds.fit_reason:
YES

The riddle is narrated by a submarine crew ("we heard the clang," "we cheered"), and it is explicitly dated September 1943, north of New Britain. It concerns their torpedo attacks and the failures of their weapons, which fits the requested setting.
